Meanwhile, an analysis found no decline in prescribed burning overall despite growing litigation concerns among firefighters who worry about accountability and criminal charges.

The report concludes by contrasting Western states' progress with New Mexico's trajectory as a cautionary tale. Climate change further complicates the landscape, with a 2023 study from UCLA finding rising temperatures will cut suitable days for prescribed fire by 17 percent on average by 2060 in the Western U.S.
items.title: Wildfire Litigation and Prescribed Fire: The Liability Threat to Forest Management

items.summary:
A landmark 2014 settlement between the Bureau of Land Management, Bill Barrett Corp., and ten conservation and sportsmen's groups safeguarded about 90 percent of the Roan Plateau in Western Colorado from gas drilling. The agreement canceled all but two leases atop the plateau, refunded $47.6 million to the company, and closed roughly 34,000 acres—about 54 square miles—to new leasing through a revised Resource Management Plan written in 2016. This compromise ended years of protests and litigation that began when the BLM first proposed permits for oil and gas development on the plateau in 2007 and auctioned 55,186 acres in 2008 for more than $114 million, then the most revenue raised from a single lease sale in the contiguous United States. Now those protections face being unraveled under the Trump administration's push to open public lands for resource extraction.

The threat materializes through this December's BLM lease sale of four parcels atop the Roan, mandated by 2025's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law transformed federal leasing from a discretionary process into a mandatory one requiring quarterly sales in nine producing states and forcing nominated land to be offered within 18 months—down from six years under prior litigation. New leases would carry only stipulations baked into the outdated 2016 management plan, barring incorporation of newer science such as a 2017 study on energy development's impacts on ungulates or new surface-use protections requested by land managers.

The Roan Plateau rises 3,500 feet above the Colorado River Valley between De Beque and Rifle on Colorado's Western Slope, atop the southern margin of the Piceance Basin—one of the most heavily drilled natural gas fields in the West. Its public lands form an island of intact habitat surrounded by industrialized private land to the west; the protected eastern side hosts emerald-green alpine meadows, streams designated as Outstanding Waters including East Fork Parachute Creek where genetically pure Colorado River cutthroat trout spawn within parcels now proposed for leasing.

The rare cutthroat strain evolved to tolerate warmer water. Dean Riggs, who retired in 2020 after three decades with Colorado Parks and Wildlife, warns losing these fish would forfeit genetics needed as waters warm. Infrastructure development removes vegetation, increases stream temperatures, fragments habitat via culverts and roads, and can displace deer and elk for over 15 years even after wells close—pressures compounded by drought, wildfires, floods, and a state that just posted its lowest snowpack on record.

The BLM's proposed Oil and Gas Leasing rule would further compress public involvement from 90 days to a 10-day protest window, eliminate balancing of mineral development against wildlife habitat value, revive noncompetitive leasing, reduce bonding requirements, and require $1 per-page fees on protests exceeding 50 pages. The comment period closed Sept. 11, with the sale set for December 8th.

Opinions diverge: Chris Winter of Colorado's Getches-Wilkinson Center emphasizes the broad local consensus that was overridden by administrative action; Wade Haerle of Club 20 argues hunting, fishing, and oil and gas can coexist. Riggs expects drilling to proceed in previously protected parcels without breaking any deal, since permanent protection generally requires Congress—which has instead pushed to roll back protections—making the Roan an early warning of a strategy targeting less permanent land designations.
items.title: Colorado's Roan Plateau: A Landmark Conservation Deal Threatened by New Federal Lease Sales

items.summary: Russia's Defense Ministry reported on Tuesday that its air defenses downed more than 1,400 Ukrainian drones during a second consecutive night of large-scale attacks. This figure represented an increase from Monday's count of 1,336 interceptions—the highest number Russia had claimed at any single point in the war—and reflected a broader escalation in aerial activity as both sides awaited a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks on ending the conflict that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022. Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces targeted the Kerch Bridge—a crucial span carrying military and civilian supplies between Russia and Crimea and also a symbol of Russia's annexation of the peninsula in 2014—for a second day running. While officials initially downplayed Monday's damage as insignificant, unconfirmed media reports indicated that Tuesday's repeat strike severely damaged one of the bridge's two arches; The Associated Press could not immediately verify whether any span had collapsed. In response to the disruption, Sergei Aksyonov, Russia's installed governor of Crimea, announced that traffic across the bridge has been halted and urged people to refrain from traveling toward it—though he made no mention of damage.
items.title: Russia Reports Downings of 1,400+ Ukrainian Drones as Kyiv Strikes Kerch Bridge in Crimea

items.summary: President Trump is traveling to Asia for a series of meetings covering trade and security matters. The trip includes a rare trilateral meeting with China and Russia, during which he will meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in a joint summit. Audio from the event was expected to be released later that day. The article contains no specific figures or dates beyond this framing.
items.title: Trump to Meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin for Joint Summit

items.summary:
Grindr, the world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app, launched its premium subscription service globally at a price of $120 (£91) per month. The company's CEO George Arison described it as "a very different Grindr experience" aimed at "a small community of users," and was unapologetic about the cost, stating: "I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not." This new tier follows existing offerings that include a free service plus two additional tiers costing between $22.99 and $44.99 per month.

The premium offering is part of Grindr's broader effort to become what it calls an "AI-first company," investing in artificial intelligence to build products more quickly and cheaply. The Edge service, which powers the premium tier, uses AI-powered features such as daily personalized profile recommendations designed to provide better matches and limit scrolling, plus insights into a user's compatibility with prospective matches and resurfaced summaries of past connections.

Grindr has been experimenting with Edge for much of the last year in markets including the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. On its earnings call earlier this month, the company reported that almost 400,000 users had registered for the service within the first 72 hours it was available for testing.

User reactions to the new pricing were mixed. In San Francisco, one user named Rybin said "The current premium Grindr tier is already really expensive," and described the newest offering as "really out of touch with the community." Another user, Adrian, added that the high cost "leaves a bad taste in my mouth." Conversely, a user named Michael stated: "The cost doesn't bother me," arguing that all apps have premium tiers and noting that high-end dating apps like The League can charge much more.

Arison defended introducing an ultra-premium tier despite concerns about dividing users into "haves" and "have-nots." He argued that Edge users being willing to pay more would allow the company to subsidize the product for everyone else, framing it as a personal choice. Arison also noted he has left open the possibility of increasing the cost in the future.

The AI strategy extends beyond Grindr's own products. In September, amid debate over AI safety across Silicon Valley, Arison said concerns about what he called an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic" prompted him to instruct some engineers to stop using Anthropic's technology. Although Anthropic is due to start selling shares to the public for the first time that week and its Claude Code tools remain in use at Grindr now, Arison said the company was on track to completely phase it out of his company's workflows by next year.
items.title: Grindr Defends $120 Monthly Premium Tier as It Launches Globally

items.summary: As India pursues its biodiversity goals under the 2030 '30 x 30' target adopted at COP15, researchers are proposing long-protected institutional campuses as Other Effective area-based Conservation Measure (OECM) sites to expand the country's protected-area network. A recent analysis indicates that India's protected areas currently cover roughly 28% of its geographical area through various regulatory frameworks—Wildlife Protection Act lands, Indian Forest Act forest lands, and Biological Diversity Act biodiversity heritage sites—which is close to but short of the 30% target; bridging the remaining gap requires shared spaces rather than conventional national parks and sanctuaries. OECMs fall under this category as a novel conservation instrument. The CSIR-NEERI campus in Nagpur serves as a case study, having been established in 1958 at roughly 46 hectares (about the size of 65 football fields), with dense vegetation that maintains temperatures about 3°C lower than surrounding areas and hosts more than half of India's bird species. Systematic sampling over a full year revealed 1,744 trees across 83 tree species, along with numerous microhabitats supporting insects, birds, and small mammals. Experts like Jagdish Krishnaswamy note that stable land tenure, established governance, restricted public access, and sustained management make such campuses strong candidates for OECM status, while India has already declared the Aravalli Biodiversity Park in Haryana as its first OECM site, with 13 more potential sites identified nationally. However, critics like Seshadri K.S. caution that OECMs lack statutory backing and face risks of becoming 'paper OECMs' or ecological sinks without committed management practices fostering coexistence among diverse fauna.
items.title: Institutional Campuses as OECMs: Expanding India's Conservation Network Amid Caution

items.summary:
Bilkis Bano, a Muslim woman who was gang-raped while pregnant during the 2002 Gujarat riots and saw her three-year-old daughter Saleha killed, has spoken of "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were granted bail. In a statement released Monday night, she said she had learned of the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back, noting that for 24 long years she had repeatedly stood up to fight for justice but now felt herself losing "the very justice I had fought so hard to win." She expressed fear of losing faith in the judiciary again and affirmed her resolve is for Saleha's memory and for women everywhere. The two freed men are Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, part of a group of 11 convicts serving life terms for the attack; both were released after being held more than 17 years, with one appellant described as having a severe handicap. Their release followed an order dated 28 October that suspended their sentences while they challenge a 2017 Bombay High Court ruling.

Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC her client was heartbroken and had no information about the case coming before the Supreme Court, warning each such event risks eroding faith in justice. The attack occurred on the morning of 3 March 2002 when Hindu mobs with swords and sticks assaulted Muslim neighbourhoods after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train at Godhra; Bano's village was attacked while she, pregnant with her second child, fled for safety. The riots continued three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims, including Bano's daughter Saleha, snatched from her lap and killed, plus a cousin who had given birth two days earlier along with the newborn.

Bano survived only after losing consciousness while attackers believed she was dead. The first arrests came in 2004 after the Supreme Court transferred the case to Mumbai, ruling Gujarat courts could not deliver justice. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, then Gujarat chief minister during the riots and criticised for failing to prevent the carnage, has consistently denied wrongdoing and never apologised; a 2013 Supreme Court panel found insufficient evidence to prosecute him, though critics continue to hold him responsible for the violence on his watch.
items.title: Pregnant rape survivor's heartbreak after two convicts granted bail in 2002 Gujarat case

items.summary: Twenty-five years after Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone premiered on November 16, 2001—when the then-11-year-old Emma Watson was chosen for Hermione Granger after about 10 auditions—the actress is marking the anniversary as far from the spotlight as possible. Born in Paris but raised in Oxford with no professional experience or interest in acting, Watson built a career that critics, audiences, and fashion industry alike embraced to avoid typecasting her. At 36, she has spent years away from acting after roles such as Little Women (2019), working with directors like Sofia Coppola, Darren Aronofsky, and Greta Gerwig, and starring in Disney's Beauty and the Beast. In an interview with Hollywood Authentic in September 2025, Watson described herself as perhaps the happiest and healthiest she has ever been while managing the aftermath of fame that arrived too early and intensely. She told the Financial Times that she felt caged and was frustrated by having to promote films whose creative processes she did not control, saying 'I didn't have a voice, I didn't have a say.' Watson also described the pain of leaving behind the close-knit community built around Harry Potter; after spending a decade working with colleagues bound by emotional ties, she found Hollywood's competitive environment deeply isolating. She acknowledged lacking the 'thick skin' needed to thrive there and felt as though her bones were being broken when she realized others focused on their own careers. During her time away from red carpets, Watson reclaimed parts of her life: in May 2014 she graduated with a degree in English Literature from Brown University, later resumed studies with a master's in creative writing at Oxford, and developed business projects such as Prada's Paradoxe fragrance (which she directed an ad for) and the premium gin Renais launched with her brother Alex. She is also a UN Goodwill Ambassador and maintains more than 70 million Instagram followers, showing sporadic commitment to the environment, the Palestinian cause, and trans rights—a stance that led to a public clash with J.K. Rowling, who called Watson 'ignorant.' Though Hermione's story returns this holiday season via HBO Max's new adaptation featuring Arabella Stanton as the young witch, Emma Watson remains in no rush to return.
items.title: Emma Watson Steps Back from Hollywood 25 Years After 'Harry Potter'

items.summary: Tobacco group Imperial Brands is cutting up to 4,600 jobs as part of a major cost-saving drive tied to its increasing use of AI and other technologies. The Bristol-based company said this year alone would see 2,100 roles eliminated globally, with plans for a further reduction of between 2,100 and 2,500 jobs by the end of 2030. Imperial Brands has a global workforce of about 25,000 people; it will close its Langenhagen factory in Germany next year and has sold a plant in Taiwan, leading to 700 job losses. The company intends to outsource 400 jobs to Capgemini from its finance and procurement teams in Krakow, Poland and its global supply chain centre in Warsaw. Chief executive Lukas Paravicini described the cuts as part of a 'transformation' targeting at least £320m of annual savings by 2030, aiming to make the company more agile, data-led, consumer-facing and efficient through new software and AI. As cigarette volumes decline, the group—which is also behind John Player Special, Golden Virginia and Rizla brands—has been revamping its business toward newer products including vapes, heated tobacco and oral nicotine. The current cuts affect only a small number of jobs in the UK. Imperial Brands' total revenues fell 1.5% to £31.7bn in the year to 30 September, while profit before tax dropped 12.1% to £2.7bn; tobacco net revenues grew by 1.7% as prices rose 5.1%, offsetting a 3.4% drop in volumes. Paravicini noted that Blu vape product sales were growing at double-digit rates in the UK and expressed support for regulation, which he said would bring more market clarity. The article also references British American Tobacco's plans to cut about a fifth of its 47,000-strong workforce by 2026, including 5,500 job cuts plus outsourcing of a further 3,500 roles affecting a total of 9,000 employees.
items.title: Imperial Brands Cuts Up to 4,600 Jobs Amid AI-Driven Transformation

items.summary: Actors across UK TV and film are to receive greater rights over their digital replicas under a new three-year agreement secured by Equity, the actors' union. The deal was reached with Producers Alliance for Cinema and Television (Pact) after years of talks following growing on-set backlash against AI use. Performers will now have the right to be paid when their digital replicas are used and to consent to whether such a replica is used at all. Approval must come from an actor before a digital double or alteration makes substantive changes to scenes involving agreed levels of nudity or simulated sexual activity, and producers may not use a digital replica during a strike in circumstances where consent is required. Contracts will now specify that permission applies only to a specific project rather than granting blanket consent over an actor's digital replica. The agreement also includes a 24% increase in pay rates for major films and a 9% increase for TV projects, alongside commitments to safe casting and audition spaces, training and reporting on sexual harassment, and adequate hair and makeup provision for artists of all ethnicities and cultures. Producers must limit access to digital replicas to those with a legitimate business need and use commercially reasonable efforts to protect them from unauthorised access, use or copying. The deal will be put to a vote among 8,000 Equity members, whose leadership recommends approval; it follows an indicative ballot last December in which 99% of members voted for industrial action over AI protections. Equity noted that digital replicas could instead be made from photography already captured during production without scanning artists. However, the union acknowledged areas a new agreement cannot cover, such as traditional digital scanning used later for effects, and said it did not establish explicit contract protections regarding using actors' performances to train AI systems.
items.title: UK Actors Gain Rights Over Digital Replicas in New AI Protection Deal

items.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) occupies a central position in the global competition for critical minerals essential to advanced technologies spanning medical equipment and military hardware, electric vehicles, and industrial batteries. As demand intensifies, the country has emerged as a focal point of geopolitical rivalry over mineral access. In this Special Issue, Mongabay journalists investigate how the contest for these resources is transforming governance, communities, and landscapes across one of the world’s most resource-rich regions. The series examines the intersection of deadly accidents at artisanal mines, international deals, conflict, foreign investment, and weak oversight as they converge to reshape the DRC.
items.title: DRC’s Critical Minerals Moment

items.summary:
Authorities in the city of Maebashi in Gunma Prefecture ordered school closures as officials searched for a bear believed to be its mother, after media reports said at least one person had been attacked. Officials captured a cub—one of two animals seen roaming residential areas—while the search for the adult continued. On X, Mayor Akira Ogawa urged residents to stay indoors and refrain from nonessential outings such as walks, warning of “an extremely dangerous situation,” especially in affected neighborhoods and surrounding areas. One person was injured; local media reported a man in his 50s suffered a non-life-threatening injury. The city’s schools were set to remain closed on Wednesday as a precaution.

Nationally, bear sightings have sharply decreased from the previous fiscal year, when a record 13 people were killed. In September alone, 1,759 bear sightings were reported nationwide, down from 4,766 cases recorded a year earlier. Experts attribute rising urban encounters to growing bear populations, declining rural human populations, and fluctuations in wilderness food availability that drive the animals into residential areas seeking food.
items.title: Bear on the loose in Maebashi prompts school closures and safety warnings

items.summary:
The article argues that South Africa's divide between its informal economy—where many people earn a living with weak or lopsided links to banks, supply chains and government systems—and the formal economy is a legacy of colonial and apartheid policies. This separation leaves small producers exposed when shocks hit, and while policy often assumes the answer is simply to formalise informal producers, the authors' research points to an alternative path: pairing organisations rooted in informal communities with those embedded in formal institutions.

The study examined what it takes for informally working smallholder farmers to reach the markets and institutions of the formal economy. Between April 2020 and March 2022, researchers followed eight intermediary organisations and 86 smallholder farmers across South Africa's Western Cape, Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Limpopo provinces through interviews and observation.

The research was led by an author who studies sustainability strategy, cross-sector collaboration and inclusive supply chains, alongside former students Mandy Rapson and Thanyani Ramarumo. Their study focused on social intermediaries—organisations that try to support small producers' access to markets but often struggle even in normal times.

The key finding was that farmers were well supported only when two kinds of intermediary worked together: a new national initiative able to raise money and deal with formal institutions, paired with long-standing local organisations the farmers already trusted. Neither could have succeeded alone. During the COVID-19 lockdowns, Limpopo smallholder farmers linked in this way kept or even grew their incomes, while similar unlinked farmers buried unsold crops.

The clearest test came in Limpopo, where 21 farmers were followed with different degrees of connection. Those linked to FoodFlow through Ga-Mphahlele Homecoming kept selling throughout the lockdown and some earned more than before; those without such ties were mostly left out—one farmer said simply they did not sell and buried all their produce.

The mechanism behind this success was trust. Apartheid deliberately separated 'white' and 'tribal' economies, and middlemen have often exploited that gap, so farmers had good reason to be wary of outside buyers. They would only deal with FoodFlow once a local organisation they trusted had vouched for it. When Umgibe's founder convened a meeting of farmers under a tree opening with a song, their trust in her was evident.

FoodFlow itself could do things no farmer organisation could: through its founders' networks it ran an online donation system within days and partnered with Oxfam and the Department of Social Development. By August 2020 it had raised more than R2 million (about US$120,000) and bought over 14,000 bags from more than 400 farmers in four provinces.

Yet FoodFlow lacked any relationship with the farmers it wanted to buy from. It needed partners—long-standing local organisations such as Abalimi in Cape Town, Umgibe in KwaZulu-Natal, Sigidi in the Eastern Cape and Ga-Mphahlele Homecoming in Limpopo—which knew which farmers had produce ready, how to collect it from scattered homesteads, and how to ensure payment arrived.

The authors call these two kinds of organisation 'bonding' intermediaries (drawing on close ties within a community) and 'linking' intermediaries (relying on looser ties to more distant institutions). The donations that funded the emergency supply chain have since gone, but once lockdown rules fell away in March 2022, so did the urgency. Still, everyone involved learned what a more inclusive supply chain could look like: farmer organisations gained contacts in distant markets and farmers saw what trusted local organisations can do.

The wider lesson concerns the informal economy itself. Much economic thinking assumes scaling requires formalisation—get small producers registered and contracted and markets will open—but South Africa's local informal institutions have carried farmers through decades of exclusion, holding up even in this crisis. The emergency supply chain worked by connecting them to formal institutions, not replacing them.

However, pairing only works with capable organisations on both sides of the divide; their sample also included three farmer cooperatives in Limpopo that had been set up mainly to access government grants and could not link members when the crisis came. A clear opportunity lies in public procurement: the government's school feeding scheme feeds millions of children daily yet mostly buys produce centrally, while attempts to procure locally—such as those in eThekwini—have often run into problems.

Organisations like the Southern Africa Food Lab and Seriti Institute have spent years connecting local farmer groups with the Social Employment Fund. The authors conclude that collaboration between intermediaries with complementary strengths offers a way to create more inclusive supply chains, noting that while a single organisation can sometimes straddle both worlds it is a lot to ask—so these experiments will be tested again by future droughts, floods or price shocks.
items.title: Informal and formal economies: lessons from COVID on how supply chains can connect the two worlds

items.summary:
L'élimination du paludisme est devenue un objectif réaliste pour de nombreux pays, et deux décennies d'améliorations dans la prévention, le diagnostic et le traitement ont réduit le nombre de décès liés à cette maladie transmise par les moustiques. Quatre avancées scientifiques majeures y contribuent : deux vaccins contre le paludisme, des technologies de diagnostic plus sensibles, la génomique des parasites et la surveillance de la résistance aux médicaments, ainsi que la surveillance environnementale et la modélisation prédictive à partir de données satellitaires. Ces progrès restent toutefois inégaux, en particulier en Afrique subsaharienne, qui représente encore environ 95 % des cas et des décès mondiaux liés au paludisme.

Les auteurs, chercheurs à l'Institut pour la lutte durable contre le paludisme de l'université de Pretoria, ont collaboré avec des programmes nationaux d'Afrique australe et constatent que les avancées scientifiques ne se traduisent pas toujours par des mesures efficaces. Trois obstacles majeurs sont identifiés : la prévision et la préparation (les alertes fiables ne conduisent pas toujours à des réponses opportunes), l'application des données scientifiques aux décisions politiques, et la sensibilisation face au changement de comportement, freiné par des obstacles pratiques et socio-économiques.

Depuis les années 1990, les chercheurs utilisent l'imagerie satellite pour étudier les conditions environnementales associées à la transmission du paludisme. En Éthiopie, en 2020, un système d'alerte précoce a aidé les autorités de Bahir Dar (nord-ouest de l'Éthiopie) à identifier une charge inhabituellement élevée et à se préparer.

Une étude menée auprès de plus de 7 500 personnes en Zambie et au Zimbabwe illustre le fossé entre savoir et action : parmi les participants adultes, 85 % ont correctement identifié les piqûres de moustiques comme mode de transmission du paludisme. Par ailleurs, 95,5 % ont pu identifier au moins un symptôme.

En avril 2025, l'Organisation mondiale de la santé a signalé que plus de 40 % des campagnes prévues de distribution de moustiquaires imprégnées d'insecticide, destinées à 425 millions de personnes, avaient été retardées ou risquaient d'être interrompues. Près de 30 % des campagnes de chimioprévention saisonnière du paludisme, qui devaient protéger 58 millions d'enfants, accusaient également du retard.

Trois fronts sont nécessaires pour combler le fossé entre la science et l'impact concret : renforcer les systèmes de santé, améliorer l'accès des communautés à la prévention et à une éducation sanitaire adaptée au contexte local, et assurer la coordination entre chercheurs, décideurs et programmes. L'article conclut que la prochaine avancée dans la lutte contre le paludisme ne dépendra pas uniquement des découvertes scientifiques, mais de leur traduction en décisions et actions ayant un impact sur la société.
items.title: Pourquoi les avancées scientifiques ne suffisent pas à vaincre le paludisme en Afrique

items.summary:
At the RE+ event, Sunkean officially launched its ETL-certified 2000 VDC TRUNK-TTM system, extending its pre-assembled DC collection portfolio into higher-voltage applications. The company introduced this product to address challenges in utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) projects, where the DC collection network affects both construction efficiency and long-term connection reliability. Across large arrays, cable routing and repeated wiring operations demand careful coordination, which Sunkean addresses through two product groups: factory-assembled trunk systems and PV wire harnesses.

Designed for large ground-mounted solar plants, the TRUNK-TTM system integrates trunk cables and branch connections into a single assembly that collects DC power from PV strings and delivers it to a disconnect box. The design supports customized configurations to accommodate string positions, equipment locations, and project-specific layouts. Its vertical cable exits facilitate branch cable routing, helping installers follow the planned collection layout. By pre-assembling components in the factory, the system reduces the number of individual connection tasks performed on site, thereby standardizing connection work across the array.

The system’s current collection architecture addresses a separate concern: localized temperature rise. Where several branch currents converge directly at one point on the trunk conductor, this concentration can lead to excessive heating. TRUNK-TTM instead uses a staged approach, combining incoming branch currents before feeding the combined current into the trunk cable—a design intended to reduce the risk of such localized overheating.

Sunkean also offers copper-to-aluminum and all-aluminum options, giving customers greater flexibility in selecting conductors aligned with their project’s electrical design and material requirements. Alongside its trunk system, the company provides PV wire harnesses with multiple branch configurations—S-Y, S-X, and S-T designs—to accommodate different module layouts. Factory assembly of these harnesses helps reduce connection errors and maintain consistent installation quality, while matching the configuration to the module layout before construction aids contractors in preparing for installation.

For EPC contractors, the combined portfolio supports planning wiring assemblies around project layouts and better managing on-site workloads. For developers, it offers a way to balance construction costs with the need for reliable DC connections throughout the plant’s operating life. Sunkean frames these product innovations as reflecting its commitment to advancing solar connectivity, aiming to help customers build more reliable PV systems that support stable, long-term operation and greater sustainability.
items.title: Sunkean Unveils ETL-Certified 2000 VDC TRUNK-TTM System at RE+

items.summary: The 103 MW Huatacondo solar plant and its 98 MW/312 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Chile’s Tarapacá region have remained disconnected from the national grid nearly three months after an August cyberattack, per pv magazine. Chile’s National Electric Coordinator confirmed it activated disconnection protocols to protect the grid while an investigation continues. As of Nov. 14, both facilities had 0% availability and were listed as forced disconnections under request SDCF 2026100475, attributed to a cyberattack on Huatacondo; however, the BESS is still undergoing commissioning, so its unavailability does not count as an interruption of commercial operations. Lawmaker Cristián Araya Lerdo de Tejada submitted two formal requests for information—one to the Ministry of Public Security asking the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCI) about notification compliance under Chile’s Framework Cybersecurity Law, and one to the Ministry of Energy seeking technical confirmation of cyber origins, compromised systems such as SCADA and BESS management systems, unauthorized access, operational/economic impact, preventive measures at other facilities, and a timeline for reconnecting Huatacondo. As of Nov. 16, no responses had been recorded by the Chamber of Deputies, and no technical findings have been publicly released regarding the attack’s origin, affected systems, or resumption date.
items.title: Chilean Huatacondo Solar Plant Remains Offline After Cyberattack

items.summary:
Congress is nearing passage of a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill that would streamline the approval process for power plants and electric transmission lines across the United States. Negotiated by Democrats Sheldon Whitehouse and Republican Mike Lee, the measure has drawn support from both clean energy advocates—who see faster review for solar and wind projects—and conservative business and fossil fuel groups seeking to cut environmental red tape. It also bars presidents from cancelling offshore wind farms.

The bill has nonetheless fractured the climate movement and drawn its sharpest opposition from tribal nations. Critics argue it weakens the 1966 National Historic Preservation Act, a key tool tribes use to protect cultural, religious, and sacred sites outside reservation boundaries. Lawmakers such as House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries condemned the bill’s failure to safeguard tribal sovereignty, while Nevada Senator Catherine Cortez Masto said she would not ultimately vote for it.

The law requires federal review of projects that could affect historic properties within a broad radius—up to 5 miles from a project and hundreds of square miles in some cases. Supporters contend this process has become an excessive burden on infrastructure, especially transmission lines. Analysts Ben Schifman and Aiden Mackenzie of the Institute for Progress cite SunZia, an $11 billion wind-to-California line that took two decades to build and required a historic review covering twice the size of Delaware.

The initial bill version sought to avoid such delays by making tribal consultation optional, defining “traditional religious or cultural importance,” narrowing what counts as a visual impact, and limiting judges’ ability to halt construction. These changes drew immediate backlash from groups including the National Congress of American Indians. In response, negotiators amended the bill earlier in the month to make tribal consultation mandatory throughout review and to prevent the government from taking over reviews when tribes are slow to respond.

Opponents say these revisions fall short, with Ira Matt of the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers—himself a member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes—arguing that decades-fought protections remain eroded. Even so, some tribal nations see potential benefits: tribes with significant coal and oil reserves may welcome faster permitting for investment certainty, as did the Apsáalooke (Crow) tribe’s 2-million-acre reservation in Montana, while others hope to attract capital for renewable projects.

The article notes that even if the bill fails, the Trump administration is pursuing its own weakening of historic review through executive rulemaking. Analysts frame the reform as potentially the largest win for clean energy companies since the largely repealed 2022 Inflation Reduction Act—though one tribal advocate warned economic gains could never justify destruction of sacred sites.
items.title: Tribal Nations Push Back as Congress Fast-Tracks Energy Permitting Reform

items.summary:
Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Greece and Austria announced on Monday the creation of a migrant deportation center in Rwanda where they will send foreigners whose asylum applications have been rejected and who cannot be returned to their countries of origin. The initiative is planned for implementation in 2027 as Brussels seeks to resolve one of its main migration stumbling blocks: the gap between removal orders issued by the 27 EU member states and those actually carried out.

The scale of this logjam is significant. In 2025, EU member states issued 491,950 return orders for non-EU nationals, but only managed to carry out 135,460 deportations — a success rate of just 28%, which Eurostat notes is the highest in the past 10 years. Reasons cited include the absence of readmission agreements, difficulties identifying people and obtaining travel documents, and lack of cooperation from some countries of origin that refuse to recognize nationality or readmit their citizens.

The Rwanda project introduces a substantial difference: it relocates to a third country people who have already entered EU territory, have no right to remain, and whose expulsions could not be executed. This follows the pattern of other European attempts to outsource migration policies, such as agreements with Libya, Tunisia, Morocco and Mauritania over the past decade.

The initiative builds on precedent but differs in model. The United Kingdom signed an agreement with Rwanda in 2022 to send asylum seekers there, but it never materialized after the Supreme Court declared it unlawful a year later due to risks of persecution or ill-treatment. Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen defended the new approach on Monday: "I believe this is a game changer" and argued that they would "regain control and remove the incentive for illegal migration." The legal framework now facilitates such expulsions since October 1, 2025, when the EU Council approved the new Returns Regulation, which allows establishing return centers in non-EU countries.

However, critics question both effectiveness and human rights. Estrella Galán of CEAR questioned whether European migration policy "should be measured by the number of expulsions," calling it "a true failure." She warned that these centers move people outside European territorial jurisdiction and away from protection mechanisms. UNHCR's Paula Barrachina agreed such centers cannot solve problems alone, insisting facilities must be temporary and no transfer occur if there is a risk of persecution.

Human Rights Watch's Judith Sunderland called it premature to speak of concrete guarantees, noting they do not know how the situation will be monitored. The agency reported that Rwandan authorities denied entry to an HRW researcher in 2024 — the fourth member refused access.

Rwanda's suitability is contested. Located in central Africa, Rwanda has undergone profound economic transformation since the 1994 genocide against the Tutsis and end of civil war. Its real GDP per capita increased by 245% since 2000 according to the World Bank, with economy growth of 9.4% in 2025 per Rwanda's National Institute of Statistics. However, on fundamental rights it has a long way to go: Amnesty International and others criticize its record.

The government of Paul Kagame, president since 2000 at the head of a Rwandan Patriotic Front-dominated government since 1994, faces criticism for repressing political opposition. Freedom House's report Freedom in the World 2026 gave Rwanda just 21 out of 100 points and classified it as "not free." The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights noted persistent prison overcrowding and limited access to health care, while Rwanda's National Commission for Human Rights reported detention centers at 134.3% capacity in its 2023-2024 annual report.

Reservations also arise within the EU itself. The European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA) warned in February 2025 that return centers cannot become detached from Europe's legal obligations, demanding individually appealable decisions and independent monitoring mechanisms. UNHCR considers them a complementary tool but recommends limiting transfers to cases where protection applications have been definitively rejected after fair procedure.

The article is published by EL PAÍS USA Edition.
items.title: EU's Rwanda Deportation Center: A Solution Beyond Its Borders?

items.summary: Ronald Drabkin's new biography aims to present the full life story of Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, who has long presented something of a puzzle. The central question it addresses is how this Harvard-educated admirer of the United States—who was reluctant to go to war—came to become the mastermind behind the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941. Drawing on recently discovered Japanese sources, Drabkin's work seeks to clarify this conundrum by arguing that much of Yamamoto's popular image simply isn't true. The book runs 256 pages and is published by Tuttle Publishing as a nonfiction title.
items.title: New biography of WWII admiral sets out to show his life story as a whole

items.summary: The global success of Nitesh Tiwari's film 'Ramayana: Part 1,' starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, has transformed a quiet hilltop in Kollam district into one of India's most sought-after travel destinations. The film's depiction of the mythical bird Jatayu fighting Ravana to protect Goddess Sita drew thousands of tourists to the Jatavu Earth's Center in Chadayamangalam—home to the world's largest bird sculpture. At its heart is Rajiv Anchal, a renowned Malayalam director and sculptor best known for the 1997 Mohanlal-starrer Guru, India's official Academy Awards entry. For nearly 10 years, Anchal trekked daily up the massive 1,000-foot-high rock to oversee construction of his vision: a colossal concrete sculpture measuring 200 feet in length, 150 feet in width, and 70 feet in height, built to symbolize women's safety and honour. Inside, he designed a multi-level audio-visual museum and immersive theatre. The film has turned Chadayamangalam into a bustling tourist hub; media reports put current daily visitors at around 3,200 to 4,000, with weekend numbers expected to exceed 5,000. Executives note a massive influx from North India, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka. Kerala Chief Minister VD Satheesan and the state tourism department recently invited film enthusiasts to visit, positioning it as prime for spiritual seekers and adventure tourists. The center operates daily from 10:00 AM to 5:30 PM (often extending to 6:00 PM on weekends), with full-day ascent packages ranging from ₹1,500 to ₹3,500; additional charges apply for rappelling, zip-lining, and paintball. Access is convenient: Thiruvananthapuram International Airport lies about 50 km away (with taxis and buses available), Kollam city railway station roughly 38 km from the site, Varkala railway station as a transit point, and Main Central Road (State Highway 1) for easy drives from Trivandrum and Kochi. The piece is by Livemint—News Desk.
items.title: Rajiv Anchal and the Jatayu Earth's Center amid Kerala's Ramayana tourism boom

items.summary: Plans for a new marine protected area (MPA) in Indonesia's Saleh Bay aim to turn nearly half of the bay into protection for whale sharks, which are classified as endangered by the IUCN. A recent population survey documented newborn whale sharks there for the first time, suggesting the sheltered bay may be a pupping ground—the first-ever such site recorded anywhere—and offering juveniles a predator-free haven rich in food to develop before adulthood. According to provincial government documents seen by Mongabay, the MPA would cover 90% of known whale shark hotspots in Saleh Bay, which lies near Mount Tambora on Sumbawa Island in West Nusa Tenggara province. The species has been monitored there since 2015 and typically grows to about 12 meters (39 feet), filtering roughly 6,000 liters (1,585 gallons) of seawater per hour while living up to 80 years and reaching sexual maturity only around age 30. The global whale shark population is estimated at 119,000–238,000 individuals; Indo-Pacific sharks make up 75% of the total but have declined by 63% over the last 75 years, while Atlantic numbers dropped by 30%. Experts cite targeted fishing, bycatch in nets and vessel strikes as key threats. KI's latest population assessment documents 174 individuals across 884 sightings, with fishers since August 2024 reporting five sightings of very small sharks between 1.2–1.5 meters long—only 33 such young have been reported in prior scientific papers. In May, the governor designated 73,165 hectares (180,795 acres) for conservation, extending an existing MPA to cover more than half of the bay's total 145,900 hectares (360,526 acres). The Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries is reviewing proposals ahead of what KI hopes will be formal recognition in 2027. Meizani Irmadhiany of Konservasi Indonesia emphasized that protecting this key juvenile habitat safeguards the species' future worldwide. Fishers have worked closely with KI on conservation and now benefit from growing ecotourism, training as guides; Hamzah, a fisher-guide from Labuan Jambu who caught a young shark in 2024, noted tourism has brought new livelihoods for those previously without work.
items.title: New Marine Protected Area to Boost Whale Shark Conservation in Indonesia's Saleh Bay

items.summary: Liam Slann and his father Brian Slann are standing trial over the alleged murder of 21-year-old William Holdback, following a drugs disagreement in April 2024. Both men pleaded not guilty to murder, though Liam Slann entered a separate guilty plea to manslaughter that the prosecution did not accept. On Tuesday, Liam Slann took the stand and told the jury he wanted to "get back" at Mr Holdback after the man swung a knife at him during an attempted drug deal in Welland, in Adelaide's inner north-west. He said his father drove him there against his wishes, that the alleged victim approached wearing a COVID mask, grabbed the bag of cocaine and stabbed toward him before the knife fell into the car. Slann described jumping out to chase Mr Holdback while trying to recover the drugs, saying he wanted to "hurt" the man but only to the extent of what happened, describing where the victim was stabbed as "very unlucky." He recalled stabbing the shoulder but said his memory became hazy afterward and that he had been in shock. Under cross-examination by prosecutor Nicola Moore, Slann addressed CCTV footage showing his father asking him where he had stabbed Mr Holdback, to which the son replied "everywhere," though he later denied saying this; Moore also put to him that he left the house with a knife in the early hours of the morning. The court previously heard that Mr Holdback was stabbed 10 times and was left crying out for help on the street. Trial lawyer Elizabeth Mansfield questioned Slann about his account, and the trial continues.
items.title: Liam Slann testifies in alleged murder trial of William Holdback

items.summary:
The United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) on Tuesday designated Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City) as a Making Cities Resilient 2030 (MCR2030) Resilience Hub, making it the first urban centre in India and the latest in the Asia-Pacific region to receive this recognition. The designation enables GIFT City to share practical approaches to disaster preparedness, climate resilience and urban risk management with cities across India and internationally.

GIFT City spans approximately 4.05 square kilometres and is being expanded to more than 13 square kilometres, including its Special Economic Zone and Domestic Tariff Area zones. Currently, about 2,500 people live in the city while more than 28,000 work there. Sanjay Kaul, group chief executive officer and managing director of GIFT City, said resilience is fundamental to the credibility of a global financial centre, noting that businesses and communities need confidence that the city can anticipate risks, protect people and sustain critical services through disruption.

The recognition arrives as GIFT City seeks to integrate disaster preparedness into its urban development. The city joined the MCR2030 initiative in July 2022 with support from the Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management and guidance from UNDRR. It has completed the first two stages of the Resilience Roadmap and is now progressing through a third stage focused on implementation. A Detailed Disaster Resilience Scorecard assessment conducted in June 2023 informed the city's Resilience Action Plan, finalised in March 2024.

The preparedness framework includes disaster management plans at the city, building and utility levels, supported by a Crisis Management Group, an Incident Response System and designated officers. The city has conducted more than 15 mock drills to test emergency responses to earthquakes and fires, maintains a dedicated store with more than 36 types of emergency equipment, and operates an early-warning system integrating India Meteorological Department forecasts, alerts from the National Disaster Management Authority's SACHET platform, earthquake reports and inputs from a local weather station. Launched by UNDRR in October 2020, MCR2030 provides cities with technical assistance, partnerships and opportunities for knowledge exchange.
items.title: GIFT City Becomes India's First UN-Recognised Urban Resilience Hub

items.summary:
Environmental advocacy groups have filed a petition urging the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to lower its drinking water nitrate standard from 10 milligrams per liter to 1 mg/liter, arguing that current levels pose a public health crisis across the country. The coalition—comprising organizations including the Natural Resources Defense Council, Union of Concerned Scientists, Prairie Rivers Network, and Food & Water Watch's Tyler Lobdell—cites research linking nitrate exposure over more than five decades to cancer, thyroid disease, fetal abnormalities, and blue baby syndrome in infants. One in three Americans, nearly 120 million people, are reportedly served water with dangerous nitrate levels, including those above the proposed 1 mg/L threshold—one-tenth of the current standard. A 2019 study estimated up to 12,594 new cancer cases annually attributable to nitrate in drinking water.

The petition's underlying science was analyzed by consulting firm One Water Econ, which produced a 43-page report estimating that adopting the stricter benchmark would cost $94.5 billion over 50 years for infrastructure upgrades and maintenance—though returns are projected at $364 billion in total benefits. The states with the largest impacted populations cluster in the West and Midwest, accounting for 62 percent of affected residents; agricultural powerhouses California, Texas, and Arizona lead this list, followed closely by Iowa, where approximately 42 percent of residents face nitrate levels above 1 mg/L.

The EPA responded that it would review the petition but noted its completed July 2024 evaluation determined the rule was not a candidate for revision at the time. The current 10 mg/L threshold dates to 1975 and was formally adopted in 1991, based largely on blue baby syndrome risk—a standard advocates argue fails to account for subsequent research linking nitrate exposure to other health problems. This reassessment effort has been politically turbulent: begun under the Obama administration in 2016, paused by Trump in 2019, restarted by Biden in 2023, and ultimately curtailed when a second Trump administration eliminated the responsible office.

The petition requests two immediate steps: an interim nitrate benchmark while the new limit is considered, plus enforcement of other federal protections like the Clean Water Act to rein in industrial agriculture. Climate change may worsen contamination as intense rainfall and flooding wash fertilizer and manure into waterways, while drought can concentrate pollutants; Des Moines-area residents already faced water restrictions for a second consecutive year amid high nitrate levels, and Illinois faces similar problems—where between 2021 and 2023 more than 2 million people were served drinking water testing above 1 mg/L. As Lobdell put it, 'People are paying with their health right now,' underscoring that the debate ultimately concerns where regulators draw the line between what is legal and what is safe.
items.title: Environmentalists Petition EPA to Lower Nitrate Drinking Water Standard Amid Cost-Benefit Debate

items.summary: The Supreme Court directed journalist Nikhil Wagle and Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut to file additional affidavits placing their explanations and apologies on record in a criminal contempt case arising from remarks they made targeting Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and the judiciary. A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi heard the matter, which was initiated on a petition filed by the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA). During proceedings, senior advocate Kirti Uppal, appearing for Raut, urged the court not to insist on his repeated physical presence, citing that he is a cancer patient undergoing chemotherapy and also has heart-related ailments. Senior advocate Indira Jaising, representing Wagle, sought consideration of her age and said she was unable to attend because of pollution; while speaking about journalism as a hugely honourable profession, the bench made a light-hearted observation before directing that any apology or explanation be formally placed on record through an additional affidavit. The contempt proceedings stem from remarks by Wagle and Raut concerning CJI Surya Kant after he declined to meet a delegation of Opposition leaders raising concerns over the Election Commission and protests in Delhi. Wagle allegedly posted an abusive remark about the CJI on X, subsequently deleted it and tendered an unconditional apology, while Raut alleged that judges attended political programmes organised by the ruling party and accepted hospitality from Chief Ministers. The SCBA approached Attorney General R Venkataramani seeking consent to initiate criminal contempt proceedings; he granted consent on October 15, observing that the remarks were prima facie scandalous and intended to lower the esteem of the Supreme Court, particularly the office of the CJI. On October 16, the court issued show-cause notices to Wagle and Raut, and at a hearing on October 28 permitted Wagle to appear virtually after his counsel reported that he had tendered an unconditional apology; Raut was directed to appear physically before the court on November 17.
items.title: Supreme Court directs Wagle and Raut to file additional apologies in contempt case

items.summary: The Supreme Court adjourned the matter concerning the relocation of the 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library (CSL) until Friday, directing that its books not be shifted in the meantime. Justice Sanjay Kumar expressed concern over how the collection was being handled, accusing the Centre of an ad hoc approach and urging respect for a heritage dating back to 1702, warning against treating two lakh books as if they could simply be discarded. The court's intervention followed suo motu cognisance of inadequate space allotted to the CSL under the Central Vista plan; it currently houses 8.5 lakh books but had been offered only two rooms in the Kartavya Bhawan-2 complex by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA). MoHUA directed ministries to vacate Shastri Bhawan, where the library is located, by end September ahead of demolition for redevelopment. The intervention was sought on 3 October after reports suggested relocation due to the proposed building demolition. Amicus curiae Senior Advocate Haripriya Padmanabhan urged a halt to the move and greater clarity from the Centre on space at the new location, requesting a breakup comparing current bookshelf usage with that of the proposed site. She also raised concerns about books kept at RK Puram in 'atrocious condition' for 15 years as part of the original collection. The court directed the Centre not to shift the books until its next hearing on 20 November, and required the affidavit filed by then be placed on record.
items.title: Supreme Court Halts Relocation of Central Secretariat Library Books Amid Heritage Concerns

items.summary: On November 17, Nvidia announced the formation of a new board-level committee to oversee its national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management. The move came shortly after chief executive officer Jensen Huang resigned amid revelations involving his personal affairs, including connections with a suspected Chinese spy, which raised concerns about potential national security risks in overseeing the company's chip exports. Nvidia stated that the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee would be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include directors Stephen Neal and John Dabiri. The committee is tasked with providing oversight for Nvidia's national security and global trade compliance programs and will work alongside independent legal, national security, and trade compliance experts. Existing internal teams—the National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team—will report to this new committee as well as interim chief executive officer Colette Kress for day-to-day operations. The panel plans to meet at least quarterly, including sessions with management and in executive session. This development follows a day earlier when the Trump administration announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies like Nvidia, tightening controls ahead of US President Donald Trump's visit to China for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has faced criticism over his oversight of chip export controls in the wake of the scandal, is among officials joining Trump on the Asia trip. Separately, Nvidia was due to report third-quarter earnings after market close on November 17. By some estimates, the company holds more than half a trillion dollars in commitments through supply and capacity backstops for chip purchases, data center leases, and equity investments—though these represent only a fraction of its market capitalization.
items.title: Nvidia Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee Amid Leadership Transition

items.summary:
This post examines whether stock markets stigmatize banks that borrow from the Federal Reserve during a financial panic, which could hamper the central bank's ability to resolve a crisis. The concern is especially acute for publicly traded banks, whose stock prices immediately reflect market sentiment.

The analysis focuses on the March 2023 bank run and compares two Fed lending facilities: the traditional Discount Window (DW) and the newly created Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP), announced on March 12, 2023. The DW accepts a wide range of collateral—including underwater bonds—and provides short-term loans against market value, while the BTFP lent up to one year against the face value of high-quality securities such as Treasuries and agency mortgage-backed securities.

To measure investor perceptions, researchers built bank stock portfolios isolating four balance sheet weaknesses—reliance on uninsured deposits, unrealized losses on securities, size of cash holdings—and capital strength. They estimated a "beta" for each bank; higher beta indicates investors became more sensitized to that particular risk. Before the run, this beta was statistically zero, suggesting relative unconcern.

Between March 8 and March 31, 2023, 34 banks made their first BTFP draw while 33 drew on the DW; 10 used both facilities. Researchers compared each borrower against 207 banks that used neither facility across seven trading days surrounding the loan.

The results were striking: after borrowing from the DW only, investors' sensitivity to uninsured deposits and bank capital rose significantly within 4-7 days, with sensitivity to bank capital elevated throughout the entire week. In contrast, BTFP-only borrowers saw no significant change in investor risk perceptions—investors did not penalize banks for using that facility.

Several factors may explain this asymmetry: differences in borrowing terms (the DW offered market value while the BTFP offered face value at lower rates), historical stigma surrounding the DW which has hardened over decades, and the fact that DW borrowing was persistent—with 48 banks drawing on it during the period studied. The authors caution that the head-to-head comparison is not statistically decisive.

The study's limitations include examining small groups of banks over just a handful of trading days in one fast-moving episode, making it difficult to fully separate what a bank signals by borrowing from why it needed to borrow. Still, the asymmetry suggests emergency programs purpose-built for specific crises may be more effective because they carry no historical burden.

The research was conducted by Natalia Fischl-Lanzoni (MIT FutureTech and NYU Courant), Martin Hiti (Ph.D. student at MIT Sloan School of Management), and Asani Sarkar, published in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York Liberty Street Economics on November 17, 2026.
items.title: Market Stigma and Fed Borrowing During the 2023 Bank Run

items.summary: The US government confirmed an investigation into Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed over suspected violations of export controls involving advanced semiconductors, with renewed scrutiny focused on the firm's alleged role in helping Chinese companies access Nvidia AI chips. The Departments of Commerce and Justice announced the matter on Monday (November 16), noting that the Commerce Department had launched its investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 after identifying suspicious activity linked to potential diversion of sensitive semiconductor technology. Investigators sought records from Nvidia in May 2025 concerning direct or indirect sales of chips to Megaspeed, and subsequently placed the Singapore-based company on a 'no sell' list in June 2025. In that same month, US officials working with Singaporean law enforcement conducted an on-site end-use check at Megaspeed and interviewed its then CEO, Alice Huang. The investigation has not established any wrongdoing or disclosed charges against the firm, though the Justice Department is leading the criminal probe alongside Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security.
items.title: US Investigation of Singapore's Megaspeed Over Suspected Nvidia Chip Diversion to China

items.summary: On November 17, 2026, in Istanbul, US President Donald Trump welcomed Nvidia's decision to establish a national security and export control oversight committee, calling the move 'a good idea' and praising it as coming from a great company. Asked by reporters ahead of a Quad meeting whether he had been in contact with the chipmaker about the initiative, Trump praised the effort without directly addressing whether discussions had taken place. His remarks came alongside questions about technology outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and other organizations; a reported disclosure of his tax records by Deutsche Bank; and upcoming talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Downplaying concerns over the disruptions, Trump said 'It's life when you're big and powerful, and you have all the money,' adding that such things happen, and dismissed worries about Thanksgiving travel following the outages, asserting 'People are safe.' On reports that Deutsche Bank had accidentally leaked his tax records, he initially responded 'I paid a lot of tax' before saying it was illegal for them to do so. Regarding China, Trump characterized differences between his commerce and treasury secretaries over Washington's approach as merely two opinions or lines of thought handled very well, expressing anticipation about visiting the country. He also asserted that the US would catch up with China on rare earth production within 10 months, without providing details to support that timeline.
items.title: Trump Endorses Nvidia Oversight Committee Amid Tax Leak and Tech Outage Questions

items.summary:
Nvidia's board of directors has established a national security and export control oversight committee in response to growing scrutiny from the United States over how the company handled exports of its chips to companies linked to China. Nvidia chairperson Harvey Jones stated that "advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," adding that NVIDIA "recognises" these challenges while affirming the company's responsibility and opportunity to lead in addressing them, with a commitment to working constructively with government and industry partners to establish a robust framework safeguarding national security. The new committee will oversee Nvidia's national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management; it is set to meet quarterly, including with management and in executive session, while retaining independent outside experts in law, national security, and trade compliance.

The committee comes amid the recent resignation of Nvidia cofounder and CEO Jensen Huang following revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Prior to his departure, Huang had cultivated a close relationship with Trump, serving as a key voice for the US on artificial intelligence while also lobbying for permission to allow chip exports to China. In connection with these matters, Nvidia launched an investigation into Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy; however, the board stated last week that it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised.

Separately, on Monday, the US Commerce Department unveiled an interim final rule targeting remote access to advanced computing chips and servers through overseas data centres. The article contains no specific quantities or figures beyond these reported events and statements.
items.title: Nvidia Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee Amid Jensen Huang Resignation

items.summary: Nvidia shares fell roughly 24% this month after CEO Jensen Huang resigned following his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, prompting Colette Kress to take over as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor. The selloff coincided with Nvidia's third-quarter earnings—the first without Huang at the helm—and amid broader AI-sector volatility driven by skepticism about hyperscaler capex plans. Despite the turmoil, UBS maintained its Buy rating on Nvidia and cut its target price from $300 to $240 per share, which still implies around 54% upside from the stock's previous closing price of $156.14. UBS analyst Tim Arcuri argued that market assumptions are overly draconian—projecting a peak in 2028 with EBITDA margins compressing by 1,500 basis points—and unlikely to hold given Nvidia's momentum for at least two more years even without Huang as CEO.
items.title: UBS Sees 54% Nvidia Upside Despite Huang Scandal and Share Crash

items.summary:
On November 17 in New Delhi, chipmaker NVIDIA announced the creation of a new standing Board of Directors committee called the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. The release stated that this body is responsible for board-level oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management. Existing NVIDIA teams—the National Security team and the Global Trade Compliance team—are set to report directly to the new committee as well as to Interim CEO Colette Kress. Committee leadership includes director Suzanne Nora Johnson as chair, with Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri serving as members. The committee is scheduled to meet at least once every quarter, including sessions with management and executive sessions.

The company framed the decision as reflecting the Board's further commitment to enhancing engagement with relevant government stakeholders and demonstrating high standards of governance. NVIDIA noted that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented national security challenges, positioning itself as the world's leading advanced computing company responsible for addressing them while supporting continued technological innovation.

In a separate development, NVIDIA, IBM, and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab) collaborated to develop a modular quantum computing codesign platform that combines quantum processors with accelerated computing systems. Under the initiative, NVIDIA DGX B200 systems will be installed alongside IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM described as its most powerful quantum processor to date. The jointly developed platform is intended to enable researchers to develop and test error-correction codes, decoding algorithms, and applications integrating quantum and classical computing.

The article was auto-generated from an agency feed and has not been edited by FPJ's editorial team.
items.title: NVIDIA Establishes National Security Oversight Committee and Partners With IBM on Quantum Computing Research

items.summary:
The Guardian's Blake Montgomery reports on the resignation of Jensen Huang, founder and longtime CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, which he frames as both a reckoning for the 'genius-founder' business model and a political proxy war within the Trump administration. According to the article, Huang resigned after news broke that he had at least three affairs—one with an executive at datacenter firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence has investigated for spying for China—and others with his own employees. The departure reportedly cost Nvidia hundreds of billions in stock market value and may cost the world economy much more.

Montgomery explains that the scandal highlights divisions between two administration heavyweights: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who argues for a hawkish posture and tighter export controls on China after Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales in contravention of US export rules; and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, accused by Bessent of failing to curb such sales. The scheme involved Megaspeed buying Nvidia chips from its base in south-east Asia—installing them in datacenters in Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia—and leasing or selling them to Chinese clients.

Both men are traveling with President Donald Trump to China this week, where Montgomery expects the president's remarks may reveal which policy path he will choose. Meanwhile, figures like Elon Musk argued Huang was irreplaceable; Trump said on Monday that 'He could return' and would not mind seeing it happen. However, reports indicate Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating him.

Montgomery notes that critics of Silicon Valley see the ouster as a repudiation of the myth of the all-knowing founder, calling it a 'long overdue reckoning for the genius-founder business model.' Alison Taylor of New York University's business school described Huang's departure as the highest-profile example she had ever seen of 'key man risk,' warning that relying on one person is 'always a catastrophically bad idea.' Huang reportedly managed about 60 people, suggesting few successors ascended through the ranks. Yet he presided over Nvidia for more than 30 years, shepherding it from a gaming chip company to cryptocurrency supplier and keystone of the AI boom—forecasting $100bn in quarterly revenue.

Separately, Montgomery discusses a spate of critical infrastructure failures across the US: an extended Microsoft Outlook outage that left millions without email or services until Saturday; a Federal Aviation Administration grounding of all flights due to a malfunctioning communication system attributed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to contractor maintenance switching from copper wire to fiber; and major outages at leading banks, primarily JPMorgan Chase, plus disruptions affecting United and American Airlines. Montgomery stresses these incidents are not known to be connected or the result of cyber-attacks or rogue AI, leaving a maddening absence of unified explanation as systems transition between old and new.

For solace, he quotes Stephen King's speculation that 'The aliens have landed'—the real reason for the ground stop—and they don't want to start a worldwide panic.
items.title: Jensen Huang's Ouster from Nvidia Becomes a Political Proxy War Amid Global Tech Failures

items.summary: New Street Research launched brokerage coverage of Anthropic on Tuesday ahead of the AI company's highly anticipated initial public offering, assigning a buy rating alongside a 12-month price target of $105 per share. The IPO is expected to value Anthropic at roughly $1.4 trillion and prices its stock in the cautious range of $70 to $78, implying about 35 percent to 50 percent upside from New Street's target. In projecting revenue above $500 billion by 2030—rising from $53 billion in 2026—the brokerage frames Anthropic as priced on the cautious side relative to mature hyperscalers and materially below high-growth infrastructure software publishers, a stance it says limits downside risk since the stock would perform roughly in line with forward revenue growth. The firm also forecasts computing capacity expanding six-fold from 5 GW at end-2026 to 30 gigawatts by decade's end, which would drive annual compute costs toward nearly $314 billion. Anthropic has already secured more than $1 trillion of long-term compute agreements corresponding to 17 GW of contracted capacity—more than half of the 30 GW New Street expects deployed—which it says signals limited major financing needs, with only about 20 percent of deployment requiring Anthropic's own capital spending while cloud providers and suppliers finance most of the rollout. Seaport Research Partners was the first brokerage to cover the stock before New Street followed.
items.title: New Street Research Opens Anthropic Coverage with Buy Rating and $500 Billion Revenue Forecast

items.summary:
On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee in the wake of the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to employees; one affair involved a woman suspected of spying for China while helping ensure higher-quality AI chips reached the Chinese market, according to reports seemingly based on US intelligence that these suspicions had been known for roughly a year.

The events have heightened oversight concerns about Nvidia and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month. The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.

Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, which will meet at least once every quarter and incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts. Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair it, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, and John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech). Nvidia already has lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team groups that will report to this board-level committee.

The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous. US President Donald Trump welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines Tuesday during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell.

The scandal has also highlighted questions about US-China chip trade. Huang was influential in persuading Trump to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other companies deemed prudent. One affair involved a woman who used to lead Megaspseed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing company and major Nvidia client suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls; intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.
items.title: Nvidia Forms National Security Committee After Jensen Huang Scandal

items.summary:
The US technology firm Apple is to stand trial in Paris beginning June 17 on suspicion of having organised the planned obsolescence of several iPhone models by preventing repairs outside official outlets. French prosecutors brought charges against Apple Distribution International and its parent company, Apple Inc, alleging that they obstructed repair and refurbishment for more than two and a half years, from November 2021 to July 2024. The alleged practice involved configuring software so it was impossible to repair or refurbish the phones outside Apple's authorised network; for example, Face ID might be disabled if an unauthorised shop replaced the camera, or the battery health feature could stop working. Affected models range from the iPhone XS and the iPhone 12, 13, 14 and 15 series to the iPhone SE released in 2022.

If found guilty, Apple could face fines of up to €300,000 plus an additional fine of up to 5% of its annual revenue — which would roughly be €21.7 billion as of publication — and compensation claims from clients. The company contests the allegations as unfounded.
