Sarma argued that portraying mortals as Shiv and Parvati is not devotion but entitlement grown so arrogant it believes itself divine, stressing humility as the foundation of greatness. The political row came a day after Rahul's remarks about his parents, Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi, at the launch of his mother's memoir Belonging: A Journey of Love.
items.title: BJP counters Rahul Gandhi over Hoysaleshwara Temple post; Assam CM joins criticism amid controversy rooted in remarks on his parents' relationship

items.summary: Several Indian states have proposed reforms to the national medical entrance examination system, suggesting that students be allowed to attempt the NEET-UG exam more than once a year and that Class 12 board examination scores receive some weightage in admissions. These proposals were submitted to a high-powered task force led by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani, which is currently examining reforms to national-level examinations, according to news agency PTI citing sources. The panel was initially expected to submit its report by October 2026, but the government has granted it additional time as consultations with stakeholders remain underway. This reporting appears in a piece authored by Aastha Jha of The Times of India, who covers politics and business for the outlet.
items.title: States' Suggestions on NEET-UG Attempts and Class 12 Weightage to Nilekani Panel

items.summary: CGTN's Tian Wei attended the APEC CEO Summit held in Shenzhen and interviewed Chilean President José Antonio Kast, who described the event as a great experience. The president expressed hope for sharing insights and achievements with countries across the region during his participation in the summit.
items.title: Chilean President at APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen

items.summary: The Business Council of Canada projects that approximately 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles will enter the Canadian market by the end of this year. According to an editor's note, Goldy Hyder, President and CEO of the Business Council of Canada, stated that Canada will permit these vehicles into its market within the current year. Hyder sees strong potential for expanded cooperation between the two nations, particularly in investment. He emphasized that Canadian businesses are no newcomers to the Chinese market, noting as he said "We've been here a long time" and stressing that they have established presence there.
items.title: Business Council of Canada: 49,000 Chinese EVs expected in Canada

items.summary:
Climate change, extreme weather and the energy transition are pressing challenges across the Asia-Pacific that no single economy can address alone. Aligned with the APEC Putrajaya Vision 2040, regional players are leveraging their respective resource endowments to build practical partnerships advancing low-carbon growth.

Green industrial capacity and technology cooperation is taking shape through concrete projects. In Indonesia, the Cirata floating solar plant—described as one of Southeast Asia's largest facilities of its kind—has come online to supply clean power to the grid; built by Chinese contractors, it demonstrates how photovoltaic technology can be adapted for reservoir sites in tropical APEC economies. Chinese battery firms have also established supporting manufacturing lines within Indonesia's industrial zones, forming integrated upstream and downstream clusters for the electric vehicle supply chain.

In Thailand, BYD's Rayong plant carries an annual capacity of 150,000 units and serves as a regional manufacturing hub for right-hand-drive new-energy vehicles. The facility has attracted a cluster of component suppliers for batteries, motors and charging equipment, nurturing local manufacturing jobs and technical know-how.

For Pacific island economies on the front line of climate risks, shared satellite observation data has become a critical early-warning tool. China's Fengyun meteorological satellites provide continuous high-frequency remote sensing data to support climate monitoring, tropical cyclone tracking and disaster forecasting for these nations. Under the China-Pacific Island Countries climate cooperation initiative rolled out in 2025, Fengyun data services are open to Vanuatu, Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea and Tonga. The satellite system tracked volcanic ash plumes during the 2022 Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai eruption and supported emergency hazard assessments for subsequent disaster responses. This service is part of wider efforts under the UN Early Warnings for All initiative to close the early-warning gap in small island developing states.

Digital tools are also helping APEC economies make regional value chains more transparent and low-carbon. APEC trade and investment working groups have piloted digital traceability systems jointly by China, Indonesia and Peru to verify environmental and social credentials of traded goods; the pilot schemes cover coffee, timber and textile products. Using shared digital standards, producers, exporters and regulators can trace commodity origins, record carbon footprints and check compliance with sustainability criteria. The framework reduces repetitive compliance checks and helps certified green goods access markets across APEC more smoothly.

Under inclusive technology transfer and peer learning during the APEC Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, delegates and industry participants stress that sustainable transition pathways differ widely—shaped by each economy's natural resources, energy mix and development stage. The Putrajaya Vision 2040 sets the long-term direction for an open, resilient Asia-Pacific community. Progress on sustainability relies on voluntary multilateral coordination, accessible technology transfer and peer learning rather than uniform regulatory requirements; economies are encouraged to share mature low-carbon solutions and tailor them to local conditions instead of adopting identical green transition roadmaps.

As the APEC "China Year" enters its Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, these on-the-ground projects illustrate a core message: shared climate risks call for shared solutions. Inclusive technology access, capacity building and collaborative trade frameworks will translate the APEC sustainability commitments into tangible benefits for communities across the region.
items.title: Asia-Pacific cooperation for a greener future: APEC's low-carbon partnerships under Putrajaya Vision 2040

items.summary:
On Monday, November 16, 2026, thousands of customers across the United States reported difficulties accessing banking services and completing transactions. The disruption stemmed from a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase that caused delays involving multiple financial institutions. An ATM machine displayed a 'not working' screen at a Chase bank in Irving, Texas, illustrating the impact on physical branch operations.

Customers encountered problems with online and mobile banking services at several major banks, including Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and US Bank. Some also experienced delays when sending or receiving payments through Zelle, a popular peer-to-peer payment service. JPMorgan Chase confirmed that a temporary software bug in its on-premise hardware systems had slowed the processing of some transactions.

The bank reassured customers that they could still access their accounts and funds, and there was no evidence that the issue was related to a cyberattack. The disruption produced knock-on effects on other financial institutions when they were involved in transactions with Chase. However, JPMorgan stressed that the incident was not systemic. US Bank noted its own systems were not directly affected, while some customers might still experience delays with cross-bank Zelle payments.

Early Warning Services, Zelle's operator, confirmed that its payment network remained fully operational throughout the disruption. The situation improved later on Monday; at around 6:30 p.m. Eastern Time, a Chase spokesperson said transactions were posting normally again, indicating that the main disruption had been resolved.
items.title: JPMorgan Software Bug Triggers Banking Delays Across US

items.summary: The UK has sanctioned eight construction and property development firms in what it describes as the first package of measures since its government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank. The sanctions target companies involved in building settlements, which the UK says are illegal under international law, with the aim of disrupting their flows of finance and ability to support settlement construction. This move comes amid a reported sharp rise in settlement construction over recent years and a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property since the start of the Gaza war, triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza. The measures follow a broader expansion last month of the UK's human rights sanctions regime, enabling it to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world. Separately, the government is developing legislation to ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements and advertising services for settlement properties in the UK. This announcement comes two days before the deadline for bids on construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem, plans which would effectively divide the West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband warned that such development would render a two-state solution unviable by cutting through the heart of Palestine, describing the status quo as unacceptable while expressing commitment to working with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority toward lasting peace. Israel has yet to comment but has previously condemned UK sanctions over West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of systematically acting against the State of Israel; in September 2024 it announced its own ban on importing settlement goods and acting against companies supporting settlement expansion, prompting a furious Israeli reaction that included closing the British consulate in East Jerusalem. Since occupying the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war, Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews, alongside whom an estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live.
items.title: UK Sanctions Firms Over Israeli West Bank Settlements

items.summary: Businesses say rising National Insurance and minimum wage costs make it harder to take on young staff with no experience, prompting support for Alan Milburn's report. The REC called cutting NI
items.title: Firms on hiring younger workers amid Milburn proposals

items.summary: The UK government has appointed Alan Milburn as chair of a new Youth Opportunities Unit, which will sit at the centre of government reporting directly to the prime minister. The unit is tasked with shaping the cross-government response to the Milburn review, reducing NEET rates, delivering the Youth Opportunity and Support Guarantee, mobilising partners beyond central government, and drawing on data and insight to improve delivery.
items.title: Milburn's Youth Opportunities Unit and reactions to welfare cuts

items.summary:
UK ministers have pledged to create an entirely new welfare system for young people, giving their backing to Alan Milburn’s 278-page report. Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the move as a “watershed moment” offering a “comprehensive vision,” while work and pensions secretary Pat McFadden endorsed Milburn’s plan for greater employment support paired with significantly lower benefit payments. The government announced that Milburn would chair a new youth opportunities unit to monitor implementation, and departmental cuts were set to begin almost immediately.

The proposed system relies heavily on state intervention to help young people into work, funded in the long term by cutting disability and sickness benefits for under-25s. Under the plan, those aged 18 to 24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, replaced instead by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing.” Milburn estimated that job support schemes would prove so costly that the entire package would save the government just £200m a year. The youth opportunity service alone would cost nearly £2bn annually, with an additional just over £2bn allocated to vocational training courses and apprenticeships, plus £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies hiring young people.

Funding was expected largely from benefit reductions: the cuts were projected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn generated through higher tax receipts. However, that money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system.

Milburn launched his review amid concern over rising numbers of young Neets—a figure that reached 1 million earlier this year, equating to 13% of young people and a higher rate than in any European country except Romania. He warned Britain risks losing a generation of young people. The proposal drew criticism from some Labour MPs and charities concerned about cuts to disability benefits; former shadow chancellor John McDonnell questioned why young people would be forced to pay for the new system without taxing wealth, while Joseph Rowntree Foundation adviser Katie Schmuecker argued that cutting sick and disabled young people’s benefits should not form part of the package. Meanwhile, Debbie Abrahams called it “an opportunity of a generation.”
items.title: Ministers Back Milburn Report on New Youth Welfare System Amid Spending Cuts and Debate

items.summary: CGTN's program Green Electrostate explores how artificial intelligence is reshaping global power demand as it transforms the world at an accelerating pace. Behind every AI breakthrough lies electricity, and AI continues to grow increasingly hungry for more of it, pushing power grids worldwide toward their limits. In China specifically, two forces are gaining momentum: the rise of AI alongside the growth of renewable energy—developments whose futures appear destined to collide as they reshape the geography of computing. The episode travels to Ulanqab, a city located on windswept grasslands far from China's largest technology hubs, yet it has emerged into international headlines as an emerging hotspot for artificial intelligence. Through this journey, Green Electrostate examines how power systems built in yesterday's world can adapt to meet the demands of tomorrow.
items.title: Green Electrostate: Powering the AI Age

items.summary: On the moving sandbars along the Teesta river in West Bengal, migrant farmers grow seasonal crops that are increasingly drawing elephants from adjacent forests. As these animals feed on the cultivated harvests, they bring people and wildlife into close contact. The river’s shifting course brings floods and erosion that continually reshape the sandbars, compelling farmers to relocate their fields and adjust to a changing landscape. Elephants track the seasonal crops seasonally and return repeatedly to the same areas to forage. In this arrangement, farmers lose crops, have their homes damaged by elephants, and endure sleepless nights guarding their fields. Despite years of coexisting with these animals, however, they receive no formal compensation for crop losses.
items.title: Migrants and elephants contend over shifting sandbars of Teesta in West Bengal

items.summary: Inside Climate News examines the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), described as the biggest rewrite of federal permitting rules in a generation, which would speed approvals for power lines to gas pipelines while requiring data centers to pay for grid upgrades. The bill faced an uncertain legislative path: after the Senate voted 73-25 to open debate on it last week and then 70-27 to cut off that revised debate, sponsors raced to pass it before Democrats take control of Congress in January. Its most controversial provision, Section 1401, makes finished permits very hard to revoke—only for fraud, court orders, or immediate threats—and could require agencies acting in bad faith to pay developers a quarter to half of what they spent. The clause is fuel-blind: it covers pipelines, LNG terminals and mines just as fully as wind farms, affecting any permit effective on or after Nov. 6. Analysts disagree sharply about its climate impact; Sen. Martin Heinrich argues the bill cuts permitting for a major power line from about two decades to about five years—still too slow for President Donald Trump to finish much, so the next president collects—while Earthjustice's Abigail Dillen warns favored industries will rush to lock in approvals no successor can undo. Climate models cannot settle this because they leave Section 1401 out: Rhodium Group projects BAAJA cuts emissions but says permit certainty was too unsettled to model, while Purdue's Kevin Kircher finds the opposite by assuming more fossil fuel production. The article notes that either way, BAAJA doesn't end the permitting wars; it raises the stakes of every win for both sides.
items.title: The New Rules of Permitting: BAAJA and Its Uncertain Climate Impact

items.summary:
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay, publishing its decision on Tuesday. The court ordered Turkey to release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament, finding that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism. It also ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation. The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately but rather within the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.

Turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights, yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in cases involving rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas. As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey as well as freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers. He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.

Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup." Continuing his struggle from Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections. A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court. His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament. Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail. After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.
items.title: Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay

items.summary: According to CNN's reporting on Tuesday, November 17, a highly classified network used by the U.S. National Security Agency for its internal communications has gone down. The agency was working at the time to understand the scope of the problem, and there was no immediate evidence pointing to a cyberattack as the cause. CNN cited five people familiar with the matter in connection with the report. When seeking comment about the reported outage, the NSA did not immediately respond.
items.title: Highly Classified US National Security Communications Network Is Down

items.summary:
At this year's U.N. climate summit (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye—running from Nov. 9 to Nov. 20, 2026—the conference is billed as an 'implementation' gathering focused on turning prior agreements into action rather than issuing sweeping new pledges. Indigenous advocates are pressing governments to follow through on commitments to secure and strengthen Indigenous land rights on about 161 million hectares (400 million acres) in tropical forest countries, effectively provide $1.8 billion in funding, and respect free, prior, and informed consent in the energy transition. These demands come amid a recent U.N. report warning that limiting global warming to 1.5°C (2.4°F)—the goal set under the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement—will be virtually impossible.

The summit follows last year's gathering in Belém, Brazil, which drew historic levels of Indigenous attendance and was dubbed 'the Indigenous COP,' though it was also marked by frustration over a long-standing pattern of exclusion. Edward Porokwa, who is Maasai and a member of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, noted that it remains a struggle to determine whether further progress will be made in realizing Indigenous rights.

Climate-driven threats have intensified recently: massive floods and landslides in Nepal killed more than 1,500 people; an intense wildfire season in Canada burned millions of hectares; and wildfire smoke in Indonesia caused thousands of deaths across Southeast Asia. A historically powerful El Niño further threatens famine, heat-related deaths, and other catastrophes globally.

Funding remains a key priority. In October, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage provisionally disbursed $21.6 million for Nepal—its first disbursement and less than 1% of the approximately $4 billion to $5 billion in damage the country sustained. Indigenous leaders say the fund must work faster.

Bianca Ranson, who is Māori and a board member of the Aotearoa Climate Action Network, attends COP31 partly to highlight the landmark climate case her father, Mike Smith, led against major emitters using Māori customary law—a case blocked by the national government. Quack Pirihi, a Māori activist speaking on behalf of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change, emphasized that for over 30 years Indigenous knowledges have been brought to negotiations, yet emissions continue to rise.

As negotiations continue through Nov. 20, advocates insist discussions must lead to tangible actions rather than mere commitments.
items.title: Indigenous Leaders Press for Action at COP31 Climate Summit

items.summary:
Rhett Ayers Butler, founder and CEO of Mongabay, argues in this commentary that independent journalism plays an often-overlooked role in conservation by providing credible information, exposing problems, amplifying local voices, and helping successful approaches gain recognition. He contends that conservation philanthropy should invest more in such reporting even though its impact is difficult to measure.

Butler illustrates the value of investigative reporting with a 2021 tip from a source in Sabah, Malaysia, about a proposed carbon credit deal covering some 2 million hectares (5 million acres) of rainforest. The relationship with that source had been built over 15 years; it trusted Mongabay to protect its identity and verify the information. Butlers notes the more troubling issue was that senior Sabah officials were negotiating with a Singapore company incorporated just two years earlier, with only $1,000 in paid-up capital and no demonstrated track record of managing conservation on such a scale. Indigenous communities whose customary rights could be affected had not been meaningfully consulted, potentially locking their ancestral land into an opaque contract for more than a century.

The timing proved consequential: a Malaysian delegation was planning to market the project's carbon credits at the U.N. climate conference in Glasgow, Scotland. When the story broke and made headlines in Malaysia and beyond, those plans fell apart. In February 2022, the agreement was declared legally unenforceable in its existing form, and by 2024 it had been effectively blocked.

Butler observes that conservation organizations spend billions of dollars every year on fieldwork and advancing policy, yet far less goes to independent reporting even though it is often how local voices get elevated. He notes that philanthropic foundations judge grantees on quantitative metrics like hectares conserved, people trained, animals vaccinated, and trees planted, while scientists can measure changes in tree cover, soundscape complexity, tiger detections, or water quality recovery. These measures reveal little about who made decisions, how they were reached, who was engaged, or what happens when the interests of conservation organizations, governments, and communities diverge.

Drawing on more than quarter of a century at Mongabay, Butler explains that much reporting occurs in places where governance is weak, public information is scarce, land and resource decisions face limited scrutiny, and impunity is common. He cites 2024 findings that companies had persuaded Indigenous communities in Peru, Bolivia, and Panama to sign agreements surrendering economic rights connected to more than 9.5 million hectares (23.5 million acres) of ancestral forests. Mongabay's reporting led by Gloria Pallares undermined the projects' claims; after learning of these findings, the Matsés community in Peru terminated its agreement and Conservation International ended a memorandum of understanding with one company.

Butler emphasizes that ecological gains alone are insufficient when conservation depends on community cooperation, since resentment from exclusion can undermine protected areas. Local journalists are often best equipped to spot tensions because they understand local politics, customary rights, past disputes, and traditional practices. Reporting relies on relationships built over years with people who would never speak to an outsider.

For philanthropists, Butler argues that independent journalism has value well beyond raising awareness: it can identify risks before they become serious and reveal shortcomings in widely accepted approaches. Funders cannot dictate which stories get pursued or their conclusions; once a funder steers coverage away from its own investments, the reporting stops being useful. The independence that allows journalists to expose problems also makes their accounts of conservation successes more credible.

He offers a recent example from Gabon: the community of Massaha campaigned to protect its ancestral forest, known as Ibola Dja Bana Ba Massaha, from a logging concession operated by a foreign company. After a scientist reached out, Mongabay asked a Gabonese journalist to investigate; Benjamin Evine-Binet's story brought the dispute to an international audience and prompted the country's environment minister to visit the site. He found irregularities in the logging company's permit and revoked it, with the community now working toward official recognition of its forest as a community-conserved area.

Butler acknowledges that journalism's impact is usually harder to pin down: stories may inform regulatory decisions months later or provide evidence for court cases, prompt investigations into malpractice, or introduce associations to new approaches. Sometimes nothing follows publication, and there are important stories whose effects can never be measured. Funders accustomed to numerical targets and fixed deadlines often find this hard to evaluate; Mongabay tracks readership and republication but also follows up with reporters and sources years later.

He concludes that much of the reporting takes place in regions where few independent journalists cover environmental issues, some investigations require months of work and reach relatively small audiences, yet they still commit resources without guaranteeing outcomes. He hopes funders will do the same.
items.title: Why conservation needs independent journalism (commentary)

items.summary:
The document centers on a podcast episode from Heatmap's 'Load Bearing' series, hosted by Allison Clements—a former Federal Energy Regulatory Commission commissioner—examining the political and practical fallout of the data center development boom. The first guest is Deb Stewart, city manager of Mason, Michigan (population under 10,000), who has led more than $80 million in public investment since 2016. She describes how a developer's inquiry about utility capacity eventually revealed plans for a large-scale data center project. Concerned by negative examples from other communities, Mason drafted an ordinance addressing water regulation, development standards, buffers, noise, and lighting before community pushback emerged—culminating in recall campaigns against local officials; five council members ultimately lost their seats over the controversy. Stewart emphasizes that Mason will not provide tax incentives or negotiate community benefits, insisting developers pay full taxes while following regulations. She highlights challenges around water usage (regulated via utility agreements), noise and vibration regulation, and the mental toll on staff amid targeted social media attacks.

The article also covers broader industry developments. Midterm polling showed 56 percent of voters considered AI and data centers crucial, with 44 local governments making restrictive rules in that election cycle. On.energy is presented as a grid-safety solution provider, claiming its medium-voltage AI uninterruptible power system has 3 gigawatts deploying across four hyperscale campuses and meets ERCOT interconnection requirements.

A separate segment profiles General Flash, an MIT spinout founded by Ric Fulop that emerged from stealth with $128 million in seed and Series A funding. The company uses 'solid-state flash electrolysis' to refine metal oxides into high-purity metals without direct emissions, building a 1,000-metric-ton per year plant in Massachusetts expected to begin production next summer. Fulop's prior ventures—A123 Systems (co-founded with Yet-Ming Chiang in 2001) and Desktop Metal (founded in 2015)—both reached $1 billion-plus valuations before bankruptcy. China controls more than 80 percent of global refining capacity for some critical minerals, though General Flash only addresses one link in the supply chain.

Weather updates mention a Pacific storm potentially dumping 2 to 3 feet of snow on California's Donner Pass and India facing Cyclone Akvan near Andhra Pradesh. Additional briefs note the Department of Energy's emergency order keeping Michigan's J.H. Campbell coal plant running, Ontario Power Generation's BWRX-300 nuclear project delays with completion expected by mid-2027, and India's electric vehicle sales surpassing 300,000 units from January to October (roughly double the 150,000 sold in 2025), though EVs represented only about 6 percent of the total market in October.
items.title: Data Center Boom and Critical Minerals: Local Pushback, Grid Solutions, and Emerging Technologies

items.summary:
This weekend Estonia announced that as of December 1 all of its border crossings with Russia would close, a decision Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said was driven by “clear evidence” that the Russian military intelligence agency GRU had been behind a failed sabotage attack on a drone factory in northern Estonia. In his post on X, Tsahkna argued the closure would reduce Russia’s ability to conduct hostile activities and strengthen efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention. Prime Minister Kristen Michal framed the move as a firm response — “the opposite” of what he said was Russia’s aim to make Estonians afraid and weaken their support for Ukraine — sending a message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry are unacceptable.

Experts, however, questioned whether closing the border actually matters in an era when hybrid warfare increasingly relies on cyber tools rather than physical incursions. Anton Shekhovtsov, director of the Centre for Democratic Integrity in Austria and a Russia specialist, noted there were no direct links between the botched sabotage operation and the border closure, pointing out that none of the eight suspects arrested was Russian — they are all Latvian nationals who crossed into Estonia via other borders. He described how hybrid operations have been “uberised,” with operatives recruited online for individual assignments; he cited the 2024 attempted assassination of Bulgarian journalist Christo Grozev in the UK, and this summer’s incursion of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig Airport, where suspects reportedly reached Germany via Serbia and Turkey. Grossfield called it a trend toward on-demand operators working remotely.

On the risks side, Shekhovtsov warned that Russian agents have strong ties to organised crime networks in Europe — he pointed to the September attack on a Starlink ground station in Poland carried out by a Turkish criminal network commissioned by Russian intelligence. Grossfield cautioned that Estonians with family or businesses across the border could be affected and become easier for spies to approach, though she acknowledged it might “complicate communication and the transport of materials” and make sabotage more expensive. Shekhovtsov suggested domestic politics played a role: while Finland closed its border three years ago, he said Estonia may have been looking for an excuse to do the same ahead of parliamentary elections in March.

The article concludes that even if the closure makes Russian operations “more complicated,” it is unlikely to stop them altogether. Grossfield noted the shuttering sends a powerful political signal but does not prevent authorities from taking more targeted measures behind the scenes, and Shekhovtsov agreed it remains probably the best way to counter Russia — though he conceded closing the border won’t prevent Russian intelligence agencies from continuing to target Estonia as they have done up until now. The piece was adapted from an original French-language article.
items.title: Estonia closes its border with Russia amid hybrid-warfare fears — but can it keep Moscow out?

items.summary:
Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear before a Trump administration committee in December that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome. The refusal extends ongoing wrangling between the White House and Cook’s legal team regarding her appearance before the panel, which the administration initially demanded for Nov 6.

Trump administration officials have required Cook to appear before the committee to address allegations that she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before joining the Federal Reserve's board of governors—a charge she denies. President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she argues those efforts threaten the Fed's independence and reflect a desire to force the central bank to cut borrowing costs.

In a letter released on Nov 17 to White House counsel William Scharf, Abbe David Lowell, Cook's lawyer, wrote that “Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing – and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence.” The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a facade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.” In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump administration from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that “the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design,” per AP.
items.title: US Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing

items.summary:
Google introduced an expanded version of its personal assistant, Gemini, powered by the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. The update is rolling out free to hundreds of millions of people across the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, letting users hand off more tasks so they can move on with their day.

The post frames Gemini as a time- and money-saving assistant for busy routines filled with classes, meetings, and school drop-offs. In one example, when its minivan's check-engine light came on, the user asked Gemini to call the two nearest dealerships and secure an early Friday morning appointment within about a month; because it already knew they drive a 2019 Honda Odyssey through Personal Intelligence, it located shops on Google Maps, called both at once, booked the slot in less than five minutes via Google Calendar, and disclosed its AI identity to the dealerships. Separately, after receiving a surprise $389 electric bill, Gemini analyzed past billing statements and found that their heat pump was running around 4 p.m., during peak pricing; using this insight plus a discount code it located through Google's Shopping Graph, the user saved an extra $10 on an upcoming holiday trip charger purchase made with Google Pay.

Gemini also integrates with Instacart via RCS for grocery orders—adding items from voice text and photos of pantry contents—and connects with more than 60 popular apps. For payments security, Google is working with American Express (coming soon), Mastercard, and Visa to use digital tokens on supported cards while preserving card points and protections, and it lets users set a hard spending cap.

On data protection, tasks run in a hardware-isolated virtual machine dedicated to each account inside Google Cloud's Agent Compute Engine, which is sandboxed and tested by security red teams. Additional layers include prompt-injection filters alongside Google Safe Browsing, confirmation prompts before critical steps like clicking "Buy," adjustable task settings, the ability to disconnect apps or delete chat history, and a bug bounty program through Google's AI Vulnerability Reward Program (AI VRP). The company acknowledges that mistakes still occur—users may see tasks fail—and invites feedback via a thumbs-down rating while it partners with major websites to improve agentic navigation. To try it, users flip the home-screen toggle from Chat to Task and can forward emails to gemini@google.com or text Gemini on Android or iOS.
items.title: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen: A Hands-Off Personal Assistant for Everyday Tasks

items.summary:
Databricks announced that Azure Databricks on Azure Government has entered Beta, marking a major milestone in delivering the full power of its Databricks Data + AI Platform to the U.S. public sector. The announcement addresses a persistent dilemma faced by government agencies and their mission-critical partners: balancing the need to adopt modern data and AI innovations against stringent security and compliance requirements that often force them onto platforms lagging behind commercial counterparts, sometimes by years. For federal civilian agencies, state and local governments, and partners whose workloads fit FedRAMP Class D, Azure Commercial is already available today. In contrast, organizations requiring a dedicated government cloud with a path to both FedRAMP Class D and DoW Impact Level 5 (IL5) authorization can now access the new Azure Government environment for Beta testing.

As a first-party Azure service, Azure Databricks is managed through the Azure portal, integrates natively with Microsoft Entra ID, and counts toward existing Azure commitments, allowing agencies to adopt it within cloud environments, contracts, and identity systems they already trust. Unlike the legacy environment, the new platform runs on the same architecture as commercial Azure Databricks and is designed to receive the full Databricks platform through ongoing releases—Unity Catalog, Databricks SQL, serverless compute, and a complete suite of AI capabilities expected to follow. Beta serves as the first release on this path, providing government teams with core capabilities their commercial peers already rely on.

Looking ahead, Databricks is actively pursuing FedRAMP Class D (formerly FedRAMP High) and DoW IL5 authorizations for the new Azure Government environment, with these expected in early 2027. Once authorized, agencies and defense partners will be able to run Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) and mission-critical workloads on the modern platform, including defense workloads requiring IL5 that are not supported on Azure Commercial. During Beta, the environment is intended for non-production workloads; workspaces built now carry forward to production at General Availability. Organizations already on the legacy Azure Government environment are encouraged to begin planning their migration, as existing workspaces, notebooks, data, and configurations remain unaffected.

The article notes that roadmap capabilities and timelines are forward-looking and subject to change, underscoring the provisional nature of these plans.
items.title: Azure Databricks on Azure Government Enters Beta for U.S. Public Sector Customers

items.summary:
The article announces a milestone in catalog interoperability between Databricks and Google Cloud, built on the broadening openness of the Lakehouse architecture. What began with open table formats such as Delta Lake and Iceberg has evolved into catalog federation enabling zero-copy access to data across multiple platforms. Through their partnership and Open Source contributions, both companies continue to advance the Open Lakehouse community.

The core capability is that customers can now access a single copy of data from both Unity Catalog and Google Cloud's borderless Lakehouse. Bringing data from Google Cloud into Databricks works through Lakehouse Federation to Google Cloud, which lets customers mount Iceberg tables managed by Google Cloud's Lakehouse runtime catalog in Unity Catalog for analysis within Databricks. These federated tables can then be queried by the Databricks Lakehouse serverless data warehouse or analyzed via Genie, which answers data questions from natural language without requiring code or SQL.

Interoperability is bidirectional: data from Databricks can also flow into Google Cloud's Lakehouse, allowing customers using engines like BigQuery to read Unity Catalog managed tables without copying the underlying data. The companies are strengthening this interoperability by making catalog metadata open, on the belief that business and governance semantics should be accessible rather than tied to a specific vendor.

In the Iceberg community, Databricks helped drive and land catalog labels — a proposal enabling catalogs to share metadata through key-value pairs (labels). This ensures a table tagged with attributes such as "domain=finance" and "status=certified," or a column tagged "pii=ssn," remains properly tagged even when federated from one catalog to another. Shared labels are described as critical for governance in the era of agents, since catalog metadata can flag sensitive data for masking and provide context to AI agents searching for assets.

The article frames this shared commitment toward open governance as increasingly important as data estates grow and AI agents become more embedded in enterprise workflows, envisioning a future where governance and business context travel with data without enterprises redefining them in every system. It directs readers to documentation on starting Catalog Federation between Unity Catalog and Google Cloud's borderless Lakehouse, links for learning about Google's catalog federation to Unity Catalog, and invites interested parties to reach out to their Databricks account team.

No quantitative figures or dates were reported in the item.
items.title: Databricks and Google Cloud Advance Catalog Interoperability via Unity Catalog and Borderless Lakehouse

items.summary:
Google Cloud was recognized for the third consecutive year as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Application Development Platforms, positioned highest overall on the Ability to Execute axis. The company says organizations increasingly want AI that handles routine work within compliance guardrails and delivers measurable ROI, with nearly 500 Google Cloud customers each processing more than one trillion tokens over the past year—much of it from heavily regulated sectors such as global banking, healthcare, and telecommunications.

Google attributes this scale to Gemini, a unified enterprise agent launched in October that brings together developer tooling (Antigravity), web, mobile, desktop, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, internal chats, and other surfaces. Rather than step-by-step instructions, users provide high-level business objectives; the agent orchestrates tools, context, and coworker agents while retaining persistent memory, understanding enterprise language, and respecting permissions across devices. Teams can package complex procedures into shared skills that become organization-wide capabilities—illustrated by Dojo, one of UK’s leading payment providers, where non-technical teams built over 600 custom agents in two months.

On model access, Google Cloud is the only hyperscale provider offering all three frontier families (Google, Anthropic, OpenAI) on a unified platform. Through its model garden, organizations can draw down more than 200 models via existing cloud commitments on a single invoice without separate contracts. Recent additions include Gemini 4 Argon for software engineering, law, finance, and cyber defense; Gemini 4 Carbon for cybersecurity and long-horizon agentic workflows; and Gemini 4 Hydrogen for everyday coding.

On cost control, Google points to dynamic model matching—routining high-volume tasks through efficient models while escalating only complex problems to frontier reasoning—as well as native FinOps controls such as project-level monthly spend caps, anomaly detection, and Flexible Savings Plans. PayPal built a unified LLM stack running open-source models on GKE alongside close-sourced models on the Gemini platform for governed access across Claude, Gemini, and Open Source.

Governance is delivered through per-agent identities that produce auditable records tied to authorized roles, isolated runtime sandboxes with Agent Gateway and Model Armor scrubbing sensitive data in real time, and direct connections to live enterprise systems (BigQuery, Cloud Storage, SAP, Salesforce, S3, Azure) so proprietary data stays within its original perimeter. UKG adopted these controls to avoid building the foundation itself.

The article closes by noting that Gartner does not endorse any depicted vendor and disclaims warranties; the report is available upon request from Google.
items.title: Google Cloud Named a 2026 Gartner Leader in AI Application Development Platforms

items.summary:
At NVIDIA’s week-long presence at SC26 in Chicago, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing Ian Buck kicked off the agenda on Monday by unveiling a suite of tools aimed at advancing scientific research through AI agents. These new capabilities let software plan experiments, run code, and verify results directly on researchers’ own systems, reinforcing NVIDIA’s framing that simulation remains foundational to scientific computing while AI, quantum technologies, and now autonomous agents work alongside it.

Buck introduced several concrete products: Nemotron for Science, which combines the open Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model with a new chemistry dataset and post-training recipes tailored to life sciences; the Rubin HPC GPU built into the Vera Rubin platform; and an expanded Vera CPU line. He noted that researchers can run these tools locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation, or their own supercomputer—emphasizing themes of data ownership: “You own your data. You own the model.”

The agent ecosystem was illustrated with several deployments. At Argonne National Laboratory, an agent built from NVIDIA’s toolkit took a single prompt to plan and test hypotheses, select simulations, and identify two new binding sites. Other examples included GROMACS—an agent developed by KTH Royal Institute of Technology that autonomously repaired broken setups overnight on a single DGX Spark—SETI Institute work at the Allen Telescope Array where an agent plotted a methanol line and retuned for Doppler shift across NGC 869 versus 896, and NVIDIA’s new Nsight AI Porting Agent, which ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting model to GPUs using roughly 150 million tokens.

On hardware specifics, Rubin HPC supports precisions ranging from FP64 down to FP4, adds sparse-data acceleration, connects via seventh-generation NVLink, and carries more than 50,000 CUDA cores—about three times as many as the prior Hopper generation. It is expected in 2028.

In quantum computing, Buck highlighted a simulation on Jülich’s JUPITER supercomputer showing that magic state cultivation could reduce operations per logical step tenfold, with work being folded into CUDA-Q. NVIDIA, IBM, and Fermilab announced plans for a co-design platform to support error-correction research; NVIDIA and IBM are pairing DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers powered by the Nighthawk chip. Buck also introduced TCBP-JOBS, a decoding algorithm that cuts error-correction computation from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.

Networking roundout included one of the first deployments of NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics switches at Lambda, which he said are roughly 15x more reliable on bit errors and link flaps. Buck also reflected personally on his origins in CUDA—a talk given two decades earlier at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa—and noted that NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries.

The announcement carried forward several timelines: Vera CPUs are being selected by DKRZ’s HLRE-5 supercomputer for early 2028 use; Rubin HPC is expected in 2028; and quantum decoding latency targets a reduction from about 300 microseconds to 10. Overall, the presentation positioned NVIDIA as an integrated provider spanning agents, CPUs, GPUs, networking, and quantum co-design—all oriented toward accelerating scientific discovery.
items.title: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck Opens SC26 Week with AI-Science Agent Tools

items.summary:
In his first public comments since his shock resignation from the tech giant Nvidia, Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as chief executive if the board asked him to. The remarks came days after reports that he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and an Nvidia executive, prompting a company investigation into his conduct. Huang acknowledged having "created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," said he owned his mistakes completely, and described an "outpouring" of calls from employees, investors and others urging him to return. He stated people had continued to reach out directly as the company navigated complex technology, market, competitive and geopolitical dynamics.

Despite this sentiment, Huang's statement did not signal a likely comeback: reports indicate Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company at this point. The AI chip giant was set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which interim chief executive Collette Kress may address the situation with Huang.

Beyond the internal investigation, Huang faced being questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead over his affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing. In response, technology executives had recently praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom and an online petition began circulating calling for his reinstatement; however, by Monday many were no longer openly urging his return.

Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter suggesting Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement. On Monday at an event hosted by Semafor, Gerstner said the letter had been misunderstood and that the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course. He questioned the facts around Huang's departure but added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board," noting that if he were on a board he would take such matters very seriously, and stressing clearly that no one is above the law.
items.title: Jensen Huang Says He Would Be 'Honoured' to Return as Nvidia CEO If Board Asked Him To

items.summary:
Jensen Huang, Nvidia's former CEO who resigned following allegations of extramarital relationships with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and two Nvidia employees, is set to testify before several congressional committees on 1 December. His general counsel, Tim Teter, agreed the same day to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview on 2 December. Congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford—who chair the House's foreign affairs committee, select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and intelligence committee respectively—issued a press release welcoming Huang and Teter's testimony into what they described as a potential breach of national security, stating that Americans need answers about Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous People's Republic of China actors to access its most advanced chips. The three congressmen had earlier signed a letter on 12 November warning Huang he could face a subpoena if he declined the closed-door meeting.

Nvidia chips are central to powering the artificial intelligence boom, and the Trump administration has prohibited selling advanced AI chips to China. Megaspeed International, where Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le) served as executive director before reportedly stepping down in 2025, bought nearly $5bn worth of AI chips and advanced hardware through its operations. The company ultimately facilitated about $12bn in chip sales in violation of US export controls. On Friday, Malaysia stated it was investigating whether the company diverted advanced AI ships to other countries. A joint Department of Commerce and Department of Justice letter indicated that the Commerce Department, under Secretary Howard Lutnick, first opened an investigation into Megaspeed on 2024 for potential export control violations, with the justice department taking over in 2025 under Attorney General Todd Blanche.

In his first remarks since resigning, Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO. Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley tech giants joined 165,000 signatories to an open letter calling for his reinstatement, a sentiment Trump has also signaled openness toward.
items.title: Nvidia Co-founder Jensen Huang to Testify Before Congress Over National Security Concerns

items.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would return to lead the company he cofounded if its board of directors allowed him, while also agreeing to appear before Congress. In a statement posted on social media, Huang acknowledged that he did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA and that he had made serious mistakes in his personal life, writing that he created problems for the Board that he deeply regrets and that he owns completely as he commits to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation. He stepped down from the company last week after acknowledging that he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency, as well as with another woman who is an executive at Nvidia; however, NPR has not independently confirmed those reports. Some in Silicon Valley have argued that Huang was pushed out too quickly and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen." Brad Gerstner, founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital—an investor in Nvidia—said Monday they don't want rushes to judgment or political pressure from the left or the right forcing a board into action before fully understanding what occurred. Lawmakers say they want answers about Nvidia's role in alleged chip smuggling and efforts to evade export controls meant to block China from accessing advanced U.S. AI chips, including questions about Huang's involvement with Alice Huang, who was an executive with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was a major customer for Nvidia's chips. In a statement emailed to NPR, Megaspeed said it conducts legitimate and lawful business, noted that Alice Huang left the company in 2025, but confirmed it is conducting an internal investigation. The U.S. Commerce Department announced new rules on Monday to prevent remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, closing a loophole that may have let Chinese companies remotely access advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. On the same day, the DOJ said it was conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed. Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors from the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1st and 2nd. Later Tuesday, investors would hear directly for the first time from Nvidia's new acting CEO, Colette Kress, when the company announced its quarterly earnings after markets close.
items.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang to Return and Testify as National Security Fallout Continues

items.summary: In his first remarks since resigning from Nvidia Thursday, Jensen Huang said he would be honored if the board decided that returning as CEO was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and America. However, reports from the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal indicate the board is not currently considering reinstating him. The resignation followed revelations that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean datacenter firm Megaspeed and suspected spy; Nvidia initially described their relationship as routine before disclosing it after she disclosed the affair to employees and the board launched a national security investigation. Government action has also intensified: the US government confirmed Tuesday morning that the commerce and justice departments have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024, though no official export restrictions had ever applied; Nvidia separately placed Megaspeed on an internal “no sell” list in June 2025 after the commerce department requested its sales records. Nvidia is expected to report quarterly earnings after market close Tuesday, potentially prompting analyst and investor scrutiny of Huang’s future at the company. In his full statement, Huang reflected that he came to the United States 53 years ago, called becoming an American citizen one of life’s greatest gifts, described NVIDIA as a once-in-a-generation company built alongside colleagues, affirmed “nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible,” and took full ownership of serious personal mistakes while pledging cooperation with the board’s independent investigation.
items.title: Jensen Huang Says He Would Be 'Honored' to Return to Nvidia as CEO

items.summary:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spoke publicly for the first time since resigning on Nov 12 amid revelations of extramarital affairs that intensified scrutiny of the company's China business. He said he "would be honoured" to return if the board decided his comeback served shareholders and employees, citing an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, partners and customers. Huang acknowledged creating problems for the Board that he deeply regrets and pledged full cooperation with its independent investigation. Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment on either statement.

Separately, earlier in the day Nvidia created a board-level National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, joined by directors Stephen Neal and John Dabiri. The committee will oversee national security and global trade compliance programs and work with independent experts; its creation was not clearly tied to the revelations about Huang's affairs. US President Donald Trump welcomed the move as a good idea.

The governance step arrives amid tightening China chip curbs: a day earlier the Trump administration said it would further restrict China's access to advanced AI chips from companies including Nvidia, even as Trump headed to talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Washington has long sought to curb Beijing's access to Nvidia's most advanced processors, placing the company's China business at the center of national security and trade tensions, though Chinese firms have repeatedly found ways around restrictions—while Huang had advocated allowing more chip exports to China. US officials raised concerns about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive and controlling shareholder of Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has been under investigation over possible diversion of restricted Nvidia chips.

In the markets, Nvidia shares pared some declines and were last down 1 per cent Monday; the crisis had erased more than US$400 billion from the company's market value by that close. The committee plans to meet at least quarterly. Meanwhile, interim CEO Colette Kress will oversee day-to-day operations, and Nvidia is due to report third-quarter earnings after the market closes on Tuesday.
items.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Signals Willingness to Return as CEO; Board Creates National Security Panel

items.summary: On Tuesday, November 17, Microsoft announced a suite of new AI models at its Ignite conference in San Francisco, positioning the effort against rivals such as Anthropic and OpenAI. The company introduced MAI Code 2, a computer programming model it says nearly matches rival performance while running at what it describes as only a fraction of the cost. Alongside this coding tool, Microsoft touted a cyber-specific model intended for a limited group of customers to help address a surge in software vulnerabilities that AI tools are increasingly surfacing, and also released new image-generation and transcription models. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft's AI chief, told Reuters that building technology tailored to specific domains is helping the company keep costs low while matching competitors and even topping model benchmarks in some cases. He characterized the overall effort not as a single product but as an ongoing system he likened to a hill-climbing machine designed to co-optimize performance and price over time. Suleyman said that recent cybersecurity concerns, including OpenAI agents hacking into the Hugging Face platform, prompted him to prioritize safeguards beyond raw capability—specifically AI alignment, which involves preventing harmful actions and ensuring models behave as intended.
items.title: Microsoft Unveils AI Models for Coding and Cybersecurity as It Takes on Anthropic and OpenAI

items.summary:
Jensen Huang, Nvidia's former chief executive who resigned last week amid revelations of extramarital affairs that intensified scrutiny of the company's China business, said on Tuesday he 'would be honored' to return as CEO if the board decided his comeback served shareholders and employees best. In his first public statement since resigning on November 12 over disclosures involving a relationship with Alice Huang — whom US intelligence agencies suspect has links to Chinese intelligence — Huang cited an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners and customers urging his return. He took responsibility for the problems he created at the board and committed to cooperating with its independent investigation.

In response to the crisis, which had erased more than $400 billion from Nvidia's market value by Monday's close, the company established a new board-level committee to oversee national security and export controls — its first major governance move since Huang left. The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former Goldman Sachs vice chair, with directors Stephen Neal of law firm Cooley and John Dabiri, a Caltech professor, also serving on it. The committee plans to meet at least quarterly, including in executive sessions, and will oversee Nvidia's national security and global trade compliance programs while working with independent legal, national security and trade-compliance experts.

Interim CEO Colette Kress will continue overseeing day-to-day operations during the transition. US President Donald Trump welcomed the move as a good idea for establishing a robust framework to safeguard national security while supporting technological innovation. The committee's creation came a day after the Trump administration announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies including Nvidia, coinciding with Trump heading to China for talks with Xi Jinping.

Nvidia has long sought to curb Beijing's access to its most advanced processors, placing the company's China business at the center of tensions over national security and US technological leadership — even as Chinese firms have repeatedly found ways around restrictions. Huang had previously advocated allowing more chip exports to China. Nvidia noted that major technology companies including Alphabet, Apple, Meta and Microsoft maintain board committees overseeing areas such as regulatory compliance, cybersecurity, privacy and strategy, whereas its new panel has a narrower mandate focused on national security — a structure more commonly associated with aerospace and defense firms.

The company also warned chip buyers in recent months that the proposed US Remote Access Security Act could expose Nvidia and its customers to legal risks by expanding Washington's oversight of Chinese companies' access to AI chips through cloud services. Huang's daughter Madison Huang, who is a senior director of product marketing at Nvidia, was closely involved in shaping the public defense of the company's ties to Megaspeed — which has been under investigation over possible diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China and potential export-control violations; the firm denies wrongdoing.

Nvidia did not have a chief compliance officer according to its 2026 proxy statement, and it was unclear whether the committee was created in response to the revelations about Huang's affairs. The company is due to report third-quarter earnings after the market closes on Tuesday.
items.title: Nvidia's Huang Signals Willingness to Return as CEO; Board Sets Up National Security Panel

items.summary:
In his first public comments since abruptly leaving Nvidia amid a scandal involving extramarital relationships—one of which involved Alice Huang, founder of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed—Jensen Huang said on Tuesday that he would be willing to return as chief executive if the board decides it is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and America. He cited an outpouring of support from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners and customers since his departure, describing himself as overwhelmed by love and kindness toward his family and him. Huang acknowledged that he had failed to live up to the standards expected at Nvidia and made serious mistakes in his personal life, while affirming his commitment to cooperating with the board's independent investigation.

The scandal traces back to November 8, when Nvidia's board opened an investigation after Huang admitted in a letter to having an affair with Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence officials reportedly concluded that she was an operative for Beijing who diverted Nvidia chips to China, though the Chinese government denied her involvement as a spy. Megaspeed had purchased about $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips.

Separately, investigations into Megaspeed continued: authorities confirmed they were continuing an inquiry that began in 2024 at the Department of Commerce, which initiated it for potential export control violations after identifying suspicious activity through monitoring of sensitive semiconductor diversion. In May 2025, Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed; in June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list. Following an on-site inspection conducted with Singaporean authorities and interviews with Alice Huang, the Department of Justice took over the criminal investigation.

Pressure for Huang's return intensified as President Donald Trump said he would not mind if Huang returned to lead Nvidia, while Elon Musk—chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla—and Silicon Valley entrepreneurs such as Amjad Masad of Replit and Tim Sweeney of Epic Games backed calls for his reinstatement. Musk argued that Nvidia without Huang could jeopardize future sales deals at a company central to the artificial intelligence race, suggesting many agreements ultimately came down to 'a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract.' Amid concerns about maintaining dominance in chipmaking and retaining confidence from cloud-service providers and AI laboratories, Nvidia also announced on Tuesday the creation of a committee made up of board members and independent experts to oversee compliance with global trade regulations and Washington's national security policies. Board chairman Harvey Jones emphasized commitment to working constructively with U.S. government and industry partners.

Some outstanding questions may be clarified when Jensen Huang appears before Congress on December 1 and Nvidia's chief legal officer Tim Teter on December 2, where they are scheduled to be interviewed by members of several House committees, including the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Representative Brian Mast, its Republican chairman, said he looked forward to hearing from them about their roles in a potential breach of national security.

The article notes that investigations into Megaspeed and Nvidia's dealings with it remain ongoing, reflecting continued scrutiny across government, corporate and political channels.
items.title: Jensen Huang's Openness to Returning as Nvidia CEO Amid Ongoing Investigations and Pressure

items.summary: The article explains that using Google products—or even navigating the Internet itself—increasingly involves contact with Gemini, by design. The more users engage with Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. Previously, options for limiting how much of a user's data was used for training were limited; until now, the only way to opt out of contributing chat contents (including attachments) to training was to disable history entirely, which also prevented users from returning to earlier conversations later on. Google is rolling out new controls that separate chat history from AI training, letting users keep basic Gemini functionality while handing over less control over their data. As these settings deploy, users will see distinct toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting retains an adjustable limit, but it will no longer be required to stop Google from using usage data for training; instead, opting out of AI training becomes a separate opt-out action that must be enabled by finding the toggle under Activity in the Gemini settings—or via Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity within the Google account. The change applies only to future interactions with Gemini: any data previously fed into Google's AI already counts as part of the training set, which can include inputs, responses, uploaded files, tool calls, location information, and data from connected apps. Google says it may retain such retained data for up to three years to improve its models, though the company notes that while it attempts to filter personal information from Gemini activity history, this is not a guarantee.
items.title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data

items.summary: Google is expanding its rollout of Tasks, a toggle within Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper. Unlike Gemini's Chat mode, which allows users only to talk with Google's AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks deputizes the app as a kind of personal assistant capable of completing basic secretarial functions on users' behalf. According to Josh Woodword, VP of Gemini, in a blog post he recently used the feature to call local car dealerships to schedule an appointment for his family's minivan and also analyzed his electrical bill. Tasks was initially launched back in May as Gemini Spark, described as a 24/7 agentic helper, and was expanded to U.S. subscribers of Google AI Ultra tier before eventually becoming 'Task Mode.' Google is now making the feature available for free to hundreds of millions of people using its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. Activation is simple: users flip a toggle within the app from Chat to Tasks, or they can send texts to Gemini or call the app to give it commands.
items.title: Google Expands Access to Gemini Tasks Agentic Helper Feature

items.summary:
Nvidia's Jensen Huang has said he would be honoured to return as the company's chief executive if its board decides to reinstate him. This is his first public comment since resigning under pressure over an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, and he described himself as humbled by what he called an outpouring of support for his comeback.

In a statement provided to media outlets, Huang acknowledged that he had not met the standards expected at Nvidia and admitted making serious personal mistakes. He said he created problems for the board that he deeply regrets, took full ownership of those errors, and remains committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation. His willingness to return follows a reinstatement campaign backed by tech figures including Elon Musk.

According to a counter on the official "Stand with Jensen" website, more than 190,000 people have signed an open letter demanding that the board re-employ him. Huang said he has heard calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners and customers for his return as CEO, adding that if the board of directors concludes his return serves shareholders, employees, the company and America, he would gladly answer those calls.

On Monday, US President Donald Trump remarked that he "would certainly not mind seeing" Huang come back to the role. Meanwhile, the United States has moved to tighten controls aimed at preventing chip-smuggling in the wake of the scandal. Ms Huang worked for a company that US authorities believe may have circumvented those controls to send Nvidia's most powerful AI chips into China.

The FBI and several congressional committees are investigating the matter. Jensen Huang has agreed to answer questions before them on December 1, according to a statement from the House Committee on Foreign Affairs. The committee chairs said the American people need answers about Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous People's Republic of China actors to access advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in the scandal. Their inquiry also involves the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee.

The Nvidia board has not officially commented on the calls for Huang's return, though Reuters and other news agencies reported that the board was not considering asking him to come back.
items.title: Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honoured' to Return as Nvidia CEO

items.summary:
Google is extending how long it retains temporary Gemini chats and conversations created with chat history turned off from the previous 72-hour retention period to around two months, according to a change rolling out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks. The company says the longer retention aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable, citing potential system failures, responding to users, processing feedback, and protecting its services and users; Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change or whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed.

The extension comes alongside new settings that separate Gemini's chat history from use in training AI models. Until now both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting; going forward, users can keep their conversations without having them used to train Google's generative AI models. For those who previously disabled Keep Activity, both new settings will be turned off by default, while for those with Keep Activity on, chat history remains enabled but training use is now optional.

By comparison, OpenAI says it may retain temporary ChatGPT chats for up to 30 days, and Anthropic retains incognito Claude chats for 30 days by default. Google's updated privacy hub notes that companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons or to investigate policy violations, and states that these temporary conversations are not used to train AI models.
items.title: Google Extends Temporary Gemini Chat Retention to About Two Months

items.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos donated approximately $198.9 million in shares—771,492 Amazon shares—to nonprofit organizations on Monday, November 16, per an SEC Form 4 filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The latest contribution raised his total Amazon stock donations for 2026 to at least 2.44 million shares worth approximately $629.1 million. This year's giving followed two earlier rounds: 1,253,797 shares on May 1 and May 4, plus another 415,580 shares on August 25 and 26. The most recent donation comprised transfers of 674,088 Amazon shares on November 12 and 97,404 shares on November 13, both described as contributions to non-profit organizations. While the filing did not identify recipients, a separate SEC filing by the Bezos Earth Fund Foundation confirmed it received the 97,404 shares transferred on November 13; the remaining 674,088 shares' recipients have not been publicly identified. The combined value of donated shares was calculated using Amazon's closing price of $257.75 on November 16. Even after these transfers, Bezos holds more than 878 million Amazon shares directly—valued at approximately $226.4 billion based on Monday's closing stock price—and an additional 5,087,266 shares indirectly through trusts and a limited liability company he serves as trustee of but has disclaimed beneficial ownership of. The transfers represented about 0.09 percent of the Amazon shares Bezos directly held before donating. Forbes estimated his net worth at $376.7 billion as of Monday evening, placing him second on its Real-Time Billionaires list behind Elon Musk. Separately, Bezos and wife Lauren Sanchez Bezos made significant charitable contributions in 2025, with the couple's estimated donations reaching $600 million; their combined lifetime charitable contributions stood at approximately $4.7 billion through end of 2025, placing them tenth on Forbes' list of America's top 25 philanthropists.
